THE TWIN PLANTS. Two ivy plants grow kindly on my wall— One from the leafy nest by Ride! Mere The other drank the dews of Greta Hall, Where Dement pread its mirror, calm and clear. And like the souls of their two Bards entwining, El2tWirle these sister-plants through shade and sun, Till, o'er my porch in glossy verdure shining, sprung from two stems, they seem to spring from one. Southey and Wordsworth, who in thought may sever? yu fame and love they bloom in Brotherhood for ever. Clawnbers's Journal. F. A. THE KING'S TRAGEDY. 711 e following verses are from a ballad by Dante Gabriel Ros- setti, on the murder of James I. of Scotland. It is written as though spoken by Catherine Douglas, of whom it is nar- rated that, finding that the chamberlain has been bribed to mislay the bar which should have secured the door that keeps the traitors back, stie thrusts her bare arm through the stanchion, and for a few precious moments—alas, too abort 1 —keeps the assassins from entering.] 'Twas in the Charterhouse of Perth. In the fair-lit Death-cbapelle, That the slain King's corpse on bier was laid • With chaunt suld requiem•knell. And all with Royal wealth Of balm Was the body purified And none could trace on the brow and lips The death that he had died. In his robes of state he lay asleep With orb and sceptre in hand; And by the crown he wore on his throne forehead spann'd. Was his kingly And girls, 'twas a sweet sad thing to see How the curling golden hair, As in the day of the poet's youth, From the King's crown clustered there. And if all had come to pass in the brain That throbbed beneath those curls, Then Scots had said in the days to Come That this their soil was a different home And a different Scotland, girls 1 And the Queen sat by Lim night and day, And oft she knelt in praTer. All wan and pale in the widow's veil . That sbrended her shining hair. And I had got good help of my hurt• And only to me some sign . She made; and pave the priests that were there No face would she see but mine. And the month of March wore on apace; And now fresh couriers fared Still from the country of the Wild Scots With news of the traitors snared. And still as I told her day by day, Her pallor changed to sight. And the frost grew to a furnace-flame Thatrbunat her visage white. And evern3ore as I brought her word, She bent to her dead King James, And in the cold ear with fire-drawu breath She spoke the traitors' names. But when the name of Sir Robert Grwine Was the one she had to give, I ran to hold her up from the floor; For the froth was on her lips, and sore I feared that she could not live. And the month of March was nigh its end, And still was the death-pall spread; For she would not bury her slaughtered lord Till his slayers all were dead. And now of their dooms dread tidings came, And of torments fierce and dire; • And nought she spake—she had ceased to speak,- - But her eyes were a soul on gre. But when I told her the bitter end Of the stern and just award, She leat.ed over the bier, and thrice three times She kissed the lips of her lord. And then she said, "My King, they are dead'!" . And she knelt on the chapel floor, And whispered- low with a strange, proud smile— "James, James, they suffered morel" Ls,st she stood op to her queenly height, But she shook like an autumn leaf, • As though the fire wherein she burned Then left her body, and all were turned To winter of life-long grief. And "0 James 1" she said—" My James 1" she said— Ales for the woeful thing, That a poet true and a friend of man, In desperate days of bale and ban, Should needs be born a King!"

The true way for the average woman to drive a nail is to OM the blow square at her thumb. Then she'll avoid bit- ing her thumb anyway. "We will be Burs !" shouted the Wexford audience, in answer. to Mr. Parnelrs invective. No, no! Be the Pigs that pay the rent.—Punch. An old gentleman having been invited by an acquaintance to go oat and see his country seat, went, and found it to be a stump in a large meadow. To snatch a victory in the sight of a multitude is noble, but to conquer daily victory in the obscurity of one's home, with no drums beating nor colours flying—that is noblsr

till. "Can you steer the mainmast down the forecastle stairs ?" asked a sea captain of a new hand. "Yes, sir, I can, if you will stand below and Coil it up." Captain didn't catechise that man any more. The envious man is tormented not only ,by all the ills that befall himself, but by all the good that happens to anoOrr. He is made gloomy, not only by his own cloud, but by another man's sunshine. Show me the man you honour; I know by that symptom batter than by any other what kind of a man you yourself are. For you show me .there what your ideal manhood is, whst kind of a man you long expressibly to be. • A recruiting sergeant, addressing an honest country Imnpkin in one of the streets of Manchester with—" Come, my lad, tho&'r. tight for thy king, won't thou?" " Voight for my king," answered Hodge," why, has he fawn out wi' onybody It is easy enough to destroy, and there are always de- fitnfers enough. It requires skill and labour to erect a; building; any idle tramp can burn it down. God alonei can form and paint a flower; any foolish child can pull it all to pieces. • It is calculated that the total rainfall in the United Btates,! exclusive of Alaska, in 1880, is an amount about double thel water contents of bake Erie and Lake Ontario combined; It is 1,796,532.612,000,000 gallons, while the surface of evaporation is about three million square miles. Among the Chinese no relics are more valuable than the boots which have been worn by a magistrate. If he resigns and leaves the city, a crowd accompanies him from his resi- dence to the gates, where his boots are drawn off with great ceremony, to be preserved in the Hall of Justice. "Well, you see," remarked the milkman, as he rattled his cans all about the cart," it's sort o' between hay and grass now, and if the milk does taste a little of turnips, it can't be helped; but I don't see how that turnip was found, in the milks. The cow must have swallowed it whole." Tue great man is be who chooses the right with invin- cible resolution ; who resists the sorest temptations from within and without ; who bears the heaviest burdens cheer- fully ; who is calmest in storms, and most fearless under menace and frowns; and whose reliance on truth, on virtue, and on God is most unfaltering. The unfaithful man is more untrue to himsrlf than to anyone else. Every promise which he breaks every trust which he dishonours every responsibility which he throws off, every rightful labour which he shirks, weakens the force of the inner law, destroys his firmness, impairs his energy, I hardens big conscience, and renders him not a free man, but a slave. In being unfaithful to others, he is still more un- faithful to his own nature; in trying to secure some paltry gratification, he has lost the richest treasure of his being. AN EXAMPLE TO FOLLOW.—Joseph William Turner, one of the greatest of English landscape painters, was one of the committee whose business it was to arrange about hanging the pictures sent for exhibition to the Royal Academy. The walls were already crowded, when his attention was attracted by one which had been painted by an unknown art'st from some distant town, and who had no friend to advance his interest. "A good picture," exclaimed Tur- ner, as soon as his critical eve rested upon it; "it must be hung up and exhibited!' " Impossible ? " replied the other members of the committee with one voice. "The arrange- ment cannot be disturbed. Quite impossible!" " A good picture," persisted the generous Turner; "it must be hung up;" ad, so saying, he took down one of his own pictures, and put the unknown Mr. Bird's in its place. l'aecTicar, RBLIGION.—The religion wanted in common life is this :—We want a religion that goes into the family. and keeps the husband from being angry when the dinner is late, and keeps the dinner from being late; keeps the wife from fretting when the husband tracks the newly-washed floor with his muddy boots, and makes the husband mindful of the scraper and doormat; keeps the mother patient when the baby is cross, and keeps the baby pleasant; amuses the children as well as instructs them ; wins as well as governs; projects the honeymoon into the harvest-moon, bearing in its bosom at once the beauty of the tender blossom and the glory of the ripened fruit. We want a religion that bears heavily, not only on the "exceeding sinfulness of sin," but On the exceeding wickedness of lying and stealing; a reli- gi,onthat banishes small measures from the counter, small baskets from the stalls, pebbles from the cotton bags, clay room thbnetptearp,erbeseated from sugar, chicory from coffee, lard m strychnine from wine, u lace from vinegar, alum from bread, and water from milk-cans. hiTsn-INlBalVesitay entered the gate IV. But there are many facts which are very hard to explain on this theory, and I am, with many others, coming to suspect very strongly that plants do, somehow or other, get considerable ndirector of the Brussels Observatory, has' which he gives the results of a new piutmbr nitrogen shed grien o nz from aeau, wt hotrehkea air. . examination of the Milky Way. M. Houzeau has studied, and determined with all the precision possible, thirty dis- tinct regions in the Milky Way, and he finds that these various centres have definite relations to the general distri- bution of the stars. He concludes also that the equatorial plane of our solar world is in the plane of this more immense circle. In a historic and critical chapter relating to the determination of the parallax of the sun, he records and discusses sixty-six attempts to determine the parallax dar- ing the period of 2,100 years, from Aristarchus of Samos down to M. Stone. DISEASE GERMS.— Our knowledge of the life-history of disease germs is being steadily increased. Buchner suc- ceeded some time ago in apparently transforming hay bacteria into those which produce splenic fever. Herr P. Grawitz also showed that certain affections of the skin and mucous membrane could be produced by fungi which seemed identical with Mycoderma vini and Oidiumlactis, but which had been cultivated. In a second communication to Bidermann's Centralblatt, an abstract of which, by Mr. E. W. Prevost, appears in the Chemical Society's Journal, he de- scribes further experiments Pencillium and Eurotunt ylau- cum have been cultivated, first on bread, then in slightly acid solution of peptone containing one per cent. of sugar, then with reduced acidity, and -finally in an alkaline solu- tion of peptone. No difference in appearance is observable, but when introduced into animals these specially cultivated and thus really altered fungi cause speedy death. ELECTRIC LIGHTING OF RAILWAY TRAINS.—An interest- ing experiment, the first of its kind, was, we are informed, made last week on the Brighton Railway, to test the prac- ticability of applying the electric light for the illumination of railway carriages. The trial was made in a Pulecan car, forming part of a special train, which left Victoria for Brighton at 325 p.m. Till the invention by Mr. Faure of the secondary battery, by which electric energy can be stored, there was a considerable difficulty in the way of the adoption of electrical illumination in trains. This experi- ment showed that the difficulty has been surmounted. The car carried 32 Fanre's cells, as they are called technically, each consisting, in fact, of two flat lead plates, coated with red lead. These cells had been previously charged at the offices of the Accumulator Company. All that was ueces- sary when darkness came on, was to touch a small switch and instantly the 12 little incandescent lamps with which ' the carriage was fitted gave out a fine, mild, equable, white light. The radiance of the lamps was shed down by reilec-. tors, fitted in the roof of the car, and it was sufficiently bright to illuminate every part of the saloon. The Brighton 'Company are about to put on, for the Victoria and Brighton service, a new special Pullman train, and if last week's trial ' may be taken as a fair example of the working of this new system, it is probable that the new cars will be fitted with the incandescent lamps and accumulators for regular use In that thin. The car on the down journey during day- light was lighted by the application of the switch during the progress of the train through the several tunnels; but on the return journey in the evening the, saloon was kept lighted the whole of the distance from Brighton to Victoria. Tim PROPOSED NEW TAY Biaroox.-.—The plans of the, proposed new Tay Bridge, prepared by Mr. W. H. Barlow, Cit., are now being exhibited at the North British Railway Offices, Edinburgh, Mr inspection by intending contractors. The new bridge, which is to be built on the girder principle, will commence on the *math aide, about 16 feet west of the former bridge. At this end four brick archea are shown next the shore, each having a span of 50 feet. The girder work then commences with a span of 118 feet from centre to centre of the piers, and is continued withten spans of 129 feet, and thirteen of 145 feet from centre to centre of the piers, until navigable portions of the channel are reached. Here there are thirteen wider spans, eleven being each 245 feet and two 227 feet each. Of these spans the first four are carried to the greatest height of the structure, and give 77 feet of clear headway above high water mark. From this point the line of the bridge commences to fall towards the north on the Dundee side, at a gradient of 1 in 114, there being one span of 162 feet, ten of 129 feet 6 inches, and one of 127 feet 6 inches. These spans carry the bridge on to the commencement of the curve towards Dundee, and 25 hmre, each of 71 feet, take the structure to the side of the proposed extension of the esplanade. Several other spans take the bridge on to the point where it is run intp the level of the existing arches. The bridge is to be constructed for a doable line of rails throughout. The fouhdations in the river bed will be formed of two wrought-iron cylinders, placed at a distance of 26 feet apart from centre to centre, And filled with concrete. These cylinders rise to the height i;of within two feet of low water mark, where brick will be iused, filled in also with concrete. The brickwork is to the 'height of 8 feet above high water mark, at which level the cylinders are connected, and made to form a solid founda- tion, topped with a course of ashlar. Rising from this foun- dation, two piers are formed of wrought iron pillars braced together, and encased with iron plates of from three-eights to seven-sixteenths of an inch in thickness. The piers thus constructed are connected with each other near the top, and the whole has the appearance of a high and strongly-built arch on which to place the girders. The principal piers are octagonal in shape, with a diameter varying from 11 feet to 14 feet 6 inches. The spans are each composed of four girders connected together, top and bottom, withfracing and Iflooring. The bridge throughout its whole length will have a parapet of between 5 feet and 6 feet in height, forming a wind guard. The depth of each girder on the piers is 16 feet 6 inches. The middle girders are 28 feet 9 inches in the centre and at the ends 20 feet 3 inches. They are of dog-back lattice form. The other girders are of plain lattice work, and are connected by brass bracing, on the top ef which the train travels as on the old bridge. At the high girders the train travels between them. The platform of the bridge is of wrought iron throughout. In the construc- tion of the new britase, the old one will be sufficiently near for anchorage and cranes.

• -*,- i TIM EXA_MINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 29, • 1881 - Av\- NOTES AGRIG. ,TURE HORTI- -1 -CULTURE, &c. . Raps AND Bans—Sir R. Cross (says the Pall Mall Gazette) ha a been deploring the distressed state of agricul- ture. The practical shape his sympathy takes is a proposal, to lighten the loads on land. Farmers will do well to re- member that the substantial gainers by taking burdens off land are the receivers of rent. Rent-payers in the end gain little if anything more than an illusory deliverance from irritation. Farmers who are shrewd enough to dedine being decoyed into the Protection "snare" should look with their own eyes into this question of alleged burdens on agricul- ture. If rates and tithes and such burdens are, on economic aud all other grounds, properly charges on rent, would it not be better to connect the receiving of the rent more directly with the bearing of the burden? A NEW OPERATION FOR SPevis.—A new operation in veterinary surgery for bone spavin has been introduced by Mr. William Hunting, F.R.C.V.S., of Down•street, Picca- dilly. The old treatments, such as firing, setoning, and punching, are superseded by a method equally as efficacious ' as either of these, and more rapid in its good results than by any process hitherto practised. The new operation con- , sista of a section of the internal division of the tendon of I the flexor metatarsi muscle. This tendon passes directly I over the bones of the hock implicated in bone spavin, and must therefore directly compress the diseased parts every time the joint is flexed. It is this depression which causes prolonged lameness. If the osaific deposit were not inter- fered, with by the tendon, nature would soon consolidate it, and lameness would cease. It is the same case with "splints ;" so long as they ate not interfered with by the tendons and ligaments, lameness does not ensue, or is of short duration. But when splints are interfered with by passing tendons they render the hoists lame and unsound. AUTUMN STOCK FEEnnen.—Although there may be plenty of grass for stock in pasture just now, the condition of grazing cattle ought to be carefully watched, and oilcake or some other artificial food be given them if they appear in the slightest degree not to be thriving as well as could be wished. Several of our correspondents have complained for some weeks past that stock do not thrive so well on grass this autumn as is the case some years, the cause of which no doubt may be attributed to the excess of rain late in the summer, and the cold by which it was accompanied. Cattle sometimes get into a stagnant, ilr-doing state at the present period before the fact is seen, and it is well to guard against such an evil betimes, as it takes both time and extra food to get them well thriving again whenever such a thing happens. It is just here where liberality in feeding, and what some people term high farming, beat the niggardly penny-wise-pound-foolish policy to the exlent of making grazing remunerative instead of a losing game. The true art of fattening stock is never to allow the animals to go back in the slightest degree at any period of their course, and a little extra outlay in artificial food is seldom thrown away. Gas -Malawi AND MANTlRE.—Agrienlturists and gas shareholders will alike be interested in a discovery recently made by Professor Wanklyn, the chemistry of which Was laid before the British Association at its recent meeting. It amounts to nothing less than this--that instead of coal being distilled for the sake of the illuminating gab, and the ammonia being removed for the sake of purifying the gas, it will pay todistil coal for the sake of the ammonia, which is so valuable in agriculture, and then the illuminating gas may be regarded as a waste product. The reversal of things is due to Professor Wanklyn's discovery of a method of re- moving- the 'ammonia by a dry process. The present method of removing the ammonia, which- is a costly one, and not adopted by small companies, is to " wash" the gas in I water, which dissolves and absorbs the ammonia. Ills then obtained from the water and sold as a manure ingredient. I Much ammonia is however lost, while by the dry process it 'is entirely removed. The product is obtained in the form of 1 a powder convanient for transit, and it contains phosphate of lime and phosphate of ammonia. A DAKOTA Fanx.—Twelve miles north-west of Fargo, Dakota, is a farm which is declared by everyone who has seen it to be a model in equipment and management, and the claim is made good by the splendid crop which it has produced this year. The owner is John B. Raymond, United States marshal for Dakota, who went to the war when he was sixteen years old, and served till it was over. The farm is only two years old, and this is the' first crop. Mr. Raymond was recently requested to furnish a few totals from his account book, and the reckoning stands as follows: —" Before we receive a return from our crop we shall have invested $55,000. That includes the purchase of our land, the erection of five barns, a dwelling-house, an elevator capable of holding 100,000 bushels of wheat and oats, all the stock and machinery necessary to run the farm, and all the cost of breaking the land, planting and reaping the crop and delivering it at the market. .We have 2,000 acres in wheat, and enough oats to keep our stock. We shall get about 25 bushels to the acre, which will be 50,000 bushels from the entire place. We shall save our seed wheat for next year, and can then sell the crop for about $59,000." That is a return of about 90 per cent, upon the investment, ' or a dividend of 45 per cent, a year, for the farm lay idle the first twelve months after its purchase. To the question, "Do you consider it an advantage to own your own stock , and do your own work ?" Air. Raymond replies:—" There are as many ways of farming as there are of going to heaven and you will fled that every farmer likes his own method' best. I consider it 25 per cent. cheaper to own my machinery and stock, and believe it is more economical to borrow money to buy stock and machinery than to hire the Work done."—New England Farther. BEANS, SAND, AND WATED.—AN EXPERimENT.—In order to ascertain what amount of nutrition, if any, beans derive from the atmosphere, in June last I planted ten horse beans' in a flowerpot which was filled with perfectly clean-washed silver sand. The pat Was raised a foot from the ground, so that nothing might be absorbed from it. In due time the plants sprung up, grew freely, flowered, and the ten plants produced 28 pods which contained altogether 54 beans. Nothing was supplied to the plants beyond water, and that 1 water is exceedingly pure. When the haulm, leaves and I pods were thoroughly withered and blackened, the Plants were removed from the sand, roots and all, and were further -dried in the air under cover for a fortnight. The ten bean plants being then thoroughly dry, weighed, with roots, leaves, haulm, pods, and beams, 1,312 grains—the 54 beans by themselves 372 grains. The weight of the ten beans planted was 69 grains. From what source, then, has this increase in weight been derived? The plants could not have fed on the sand in-the flowerpot, and the water sup- plied being practically pare would contribute nothing ; and yet this 69 grains of beanseed expands to 1,312 grains of organic substance, or nineteen times its original weight in less than' three months. The 28 pods were found to contain 54 beans, and these weighed 327 grains, or nearly five and a half times more than the weight of the seed sown. Simul- taneously with the above experiment I planted ten horse 1 beaus in another flowerpot filled with clean-washed silver sand, this pot also being raised clear of the ground. These plants were watered with a weak solution of a manure corn- 'posed of superphosphate of lime, muriate of potash, and sulphate of lime. They grew freely, flowered, and the ten plants produced 48 pods. When the haulms had withered, the plants were removed with their roots from the sand and dried 'thoroughly in the air. They then weighed 3.237 grains, or 47 times more than the weight of the seed sown. The 48 pods contained 132 beans, and these weighed 1,050 grains, or more than 15 times more than the weight of the avid sAwn, , It will be observed that this manure contained I no nitrogen and yet it raised the yield of bens in weight threefold, nitrogen, as is well known, beans are rich in nitrogen. Should any of your readers care to repeat tha experiment, I "give the composition of the manure and weight per acre :—Calcic .superphosphate 33 per cent.; 3521ba. ; muriate potash 80 pet cent., 1761b5. ; .calcined 1 gypsum, 3521b5. ; total, 8801b6.—which will cost 30s. 10d, i per acre. I have found this manure excellent for cloves' or 1 vetches on a large scale. It is very economical, and can easily be prepared by any intelligent farmer. By calcula- I tions I have made I find that if the clover or vetches-1 after the first cut, which is made into hay—are ploughed in green a supply of nearly 1001bs. of nitrogen per acre is secured. The money value of nitrogen is la. per pound when purchased as sulphate of ammonia,-Peruvian guano, &c. One hundred pounds of nitrogen is therefore equal to a gain of £5 per acre, which the farmer may procure for himself from the atmosphere instead of purchasing it. Fifty pounds of nitrogen per acre is an ample supply of that element for a wheat crop, and Mr. Front only provides 3811bs.—Cold Clay. PICELED EGGS.—As butter is pickled when it is plentiful, in anticipation of the dry season when it shall be scarce and high, so eggs are packed by the thousands of dozens when they are down to about 18 or 20 cents, preparatory to the time when from 40 to 50 cents per dozen will have to be paid for a fresh article. Some of the largest bakers pack down enormous quantities, generally in lime, which is also a favourite preservative with some of the commission houses. The eggs are simply placed loose in a barrel, then lime is mixed with water and poured into the barrel until it is full, when it is covered over and left until the market has advanced 100 per cent. or more, when its contents are drawn upon. The eggs come forth, in outward appearance, as fresh as though laid but an hour previously, and the candle shows them to be beautifully clear—the action of the lime end the water keeping the air from them, have pre- vented them from changing in the slightest degree since their immersion. THE SALTING OF CriEESE.—A contemporary remarks that at Lancaster cheese fair there was a general complaint amongst the North-country buyers—who like to stock them- selves at this fair with a supply sufficient to last them till the next fair in May—of the want of good keeping cheese— as they remarked, "cheese of the old-fashioned sort, with firm, clear crusts." This well-founded complaint arises from a fresh mode of salting adopted many years ago, since which the character of Lancashire cheese for storing has become very bad. Formerly the cheese of this country were "brined "—floated in a pickle—and this rendered flys crusts close and firm, and such cheese of well-made work, like the Scotch Cheddars (which have in past years greatly supplanted Lancashire in the North of England markets), keep over a very lengthened period. A very large weight of the cheese made in Lancashire are so soft in the crusts that they need to pass quickly out of the farmer's room to the cutting counter, being difficult to carry, and unsuitable for keeping beyond a very few weeks. . ----- , ADVICE TO MOTHERS I—Are you broken in your rest by a Sick child suffering With the pain of cutting teeth? Burnley tramways have only been used six weeks, but already six accidents have occurred four of them terminating fatally. A tailor named Williams has attempted to murder his mother-in-law at Ashton-under-Lyne, and afterwards coin-

mitted auicide. Victoria Station, Manchester, has for some time been fun- minted with the electric light. The London-roa4 Station is new to be similarly lighted. At the Uxbridge Pelice-coart, on Seturday., Captain Wm. Credmer,of Highbridge, was committed for trial for the man- slaughter of his child, aged two years by fracturing its skull with a poker. The career of the adventuress—Mabel Wilberforce—has beea brought to a check. She was on Monday found guilty of phrjury, and Mr. Justice Hawkins sentenced her to nine months' imprisonment. ' Sir W. V. Harcourt (the Home Secretary) was on Tuesday presented with the freedom of the city of Glasgow. In the evening the right hon. Baronet addressed a great meeting, and in the course of his speech reviewed the policy, of the Cabinet both in foreign and domestic affeirs. , Major Bond, the Chief Constable of Birmingham reported to the Watch Committee that there were twenty-threepublic houses in Birmingham which were the resort of prize lighters and abettors of prize fighting, and where spearing perform- ances took place. The Committee ordered the police to exercise a strict supervision of these houses, and to inform the landlords that they were being watched. Mr. Bright has yielded to an urgent invitation from a body of his fellow-townsmen of Rochdale that he would accept a congratulatory addrees on the occasion of his approaching 70th birthday. The interesting anniversary falls on the 16th November, but the date of the public gathering which is to be held will bedecided by considerations for Mr. Bright's convenience. A case of suspected poisoning is reported from Birmingham. Some days ago an inquest was opened on the body of Mrs. Rollason, widow lady, who died under suspicious circum- stances. The coroner ordered the stomach to be chemically examined and Dr. Hill, county analyst, reports that the contents are strongly impregnated with strychnine, and that there are no circumstances to point to her having committed suicide. Mr. Osborne Morgan M.P., (the Deputy Judge Advocate General) addressed a meeting of his constituents on Tuesday on the Irish question. He strongly denounced the "mongrel Irishmen whose ruling passion was not love of Irelaad but hatred of England," and characterised the "No Rent" manifesto as one of the meanest and most _demoralising documents that had been issued since the time of Jack Cade. The Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol began his visita- tion of the archdeaconry of Bristol, on Tuesday in Bristol Cathedral, and inaugurated what his lordship calls a "re- formed visitation." In order to make the visitation more practically useful he has invited the clergy of the arch- deaconry to attends synod in the chapter house this after- noon, and has suggested for their discussion the question of lay help. At Blackburn, on Tuesday, Sarah Margerison, the wife of the landlord of the Whalley Range inn, was charged with stealing a table cloth and a yard and a half of cotton from the shop of William Wilson, on Monday. The chief con- stable stated that on searching the house of the prisoner a large quantity of new shawls and dress pieces were found. The prisoner was remanded, and an application for her ad- mission to bail was refused. At a meeting of the Birmingham Watch Committee, on Tuesday, Major Bond, chief 'of police, reported that there were 23 public-houses in Birmingham which wereabe resort of prize fighters and abetters of prize fighting, and where sparring performances took place. The committee ordered the police to exercise a legal supervision over these houses, and to inform the landlords they were being watched. On Saturday evening, a meeting, convened by the com- mittee of the Twelve Hours' Labour League was helelan London, to consider what steps should be taken to reduce the work hours of shop assistants and others. It was stated that since the scheme in this direction had been started a large number of employers had given in their adhesion to its objects. In the meanwhile, the committee have made arrangements to hold a series of meetings on the question. Public Baths, wjach have been erected at a cost of i 4,000, were opened at Leigh on Saturday, by Mr. Rd. Greenhough, chairman of the Local Board. Mr. T. T, Hayes, jun., chair- man of the Baths Committee, stated that by pumping from the red sandstone the water from the plunge bath would cost less than id. per 1,000 gallons as against Pd. if taken from the town's supply. Mr. Alderman Bailey, of Salford, and other gentleman delivrred addresses, and a swimming enterJ tainment followed. Speaking on Monday, in Wolverhampton, at the opening of an industrial school by the School Board, Mr. H. H. Fowler, M.P., observed that he was in a position to state that the actual number of children sent to prison had, through the efforts of the Home Secretary, been reduced' almost to a minimum. Sir William Harcourt had ordered that whenever any child under 14 was committed to prison, for however short alerm, full particulars were to be for- warded to the Home Office, and the case was then investiga- ted by Sir William in person. Father Peter Gallwey, for many years the bead of the Jesuit Order in Great Britain, has, in consequence of ill-health, resigned that position, and also the Rectorship of the headqtiarters of the Society of Jesus in England—the church in Farm-street, Berkeley- square, London. His successor will be the Rev. Henry Jas. Coleridge (brother of Lord Coleridge), or the present Rector of the Jesuit House, Manresa, Roehanapton, the Rev. Father George Porter. The number of schools, seminaries, and bhurches in connection with the Order in this country has been very considerably increased within the last few years, In consequence of the large influx of French and German Jesuits aompelled to leave those countries by reason of recent laws. Tse niOtIE OFFICE AND THE SALVATION ARMY.—Ths Exeter magistrates having prohibited the processions of the ;Salvation Army, on the ground that they would lead to a "leeeacle of the peace, Captain Davey the leader of the Army, has written to the magistrates denying their right to stop the processions, and stating that be is authorised to say that any Corporation which attempted by force to interfere with the members of the Army when taking part in such proces- sions would be held responsible to the law. He denies the power of any Home Office official to altar the law of the land, and will give the police notice of intending processions, so that the law can be tested; but in view of the utter prostra- tion of law and order arising from the idea that the Army ' was not entitled to the benefit of the law, the processions would be stopped for the present. • POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH STAMPS.—The fallowing official notification has been issued by the Post Master-General "The assimilation of the peony adhesive stamps for postal and inland revenue charges having been received by the public with much satisfaction, it has been decided to pro-' ceed further in the same direction, and to abolish the dis- tinctive stamps now used for the payment of the charges upon telegraph messages. On and after the let November, therefore, the use of distinctive telegraph stamps will be discontinued, and postage stamps of all amounts, including the penny postage and inland revenue stamp, will be avail- able for the payment of telegraph charges. This measure will facilitate the posting of telegrams in letter boxes during the niaht, or where there is no telegraph office within a con- venient .distance, as telegrams thus posted will be conveyed, without extra charge, at the next collection of letters, to the nearest telegraph office Which is open, for the purpose of being transmitted by the wires at the earliest possible moment. In those bases in which difficulty would be ex- perienced in obtaining a printed telegraph message form, ordinary paper may be used. The message may, or may• not, at the option of the sender, be enclosed in an envelope, but if an envelope is used it must be marked 'Telegram, immediate.' The stock of telegram stamps and stamped telegraph forms in the bands of the public may still be used for telegraph purposes, but not for postage or inland revenue payments." A "mass meeting" called by the Democratic Federation to petition against the arrest of the leaders of the Irish people was held in Trafalgar Square on Saturday night. An unruly crowd of about 1,000 assembled, and the majority appeared to be rather 'opposed than otherwise to the object of the demonstration. During the speaking the people amused themselves by singing snatches of English national airs, and when the friends of Federation dispersed attempts were made to get up counter demonstrations. There were several lively scenes in the Square, but the aid of the police was not required. The London Land Leagues met in Holborn on Saturday night to protest against the suppres- sion of the League. A brother of Mr. Redmond, M.P., moved a resolution expressing indignation at the imprison- ment of the Irish leaders and the suppression of the Land League, and calling upon Mr. Gladstone to undo at the earliest opportunity his recent unconstitutional acts. This having having been passed the audience rose and cheered for "the patriots in Kilmainham." The meeting in Hyde Park on Sunday was orderly and lasted but a short time. The crowd collected before the arrival of the Irish procession was composed chiefly of the class of people who are usually in the Park on Sunday afternoons. Mr. O'Donnell, M.P., who was the chief speaker at one of the platforms, made a fierce attack upon the Premier, Mr. Forster, and Mr. Bright. There , was a large meeting at Newcastle-on-Tyne on Saturday ' night to protest against the coercive policy flow being pur- sued in Ireland. Mr. Barry, M.P., declared that there was not a vestige of the! British Constitution left in Ireland, and said it was evident after Mr. Gladstone's speech that anyl species of tyranny was possible in Ireland. He urged each of his hearers to send a day's wages to Ireland, and to struggle to the end for the total abolition of landlordism. At a meeting of Irishmen held at Salford on Sunday it was resolved to form a branch of the Ladies' Land League. A resolution was passed denouncing the arrest of Mr. Parnell and other Irishmen and calling upon the people of Ireland to pay no rent until Mr. Parnell is released. Mr. Patrick Egan, telegraphing from Paris, says that Archbishop Croke is in error in his statements respecting the original "plat- form" of the Land League. Mr. Egan says the " platforia" proposed to abolish rents and get rid of the landlord system, and he declares that "the Executive of the Land League have long and carefully considered the advisability af. strike against rents, and believe such a course the only wise and courageous one to meet the present emergency." FROM A SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT. The sad tidings of President Garfield's death reached Liverpool on the morning of my departure, and the news- boys were soon crying in the streets special editions of the Liverpool papers. The stars and stripes drooped sadly from the American Consulate, and the flags throughout the city were at half mast. On my arrival at Boston, I found the eity draped in black. Portraits of Garfield were to be seen everywhere; and on the principal public buildings, such as the City Hill, State House, Post Office, and in front of many churches appeared the United States flag, festooned withblack and white drapery. Many large factories and ware houses had adopted the same funereal decorations, ac- companied by short emblematic sentences indicative of the nation's sorrow. That sorrow has been real and genuine. No man since Lincoln has held such a place in the national affections as President Garfield. He was believed by the great majority of the nation to be incorruptible. He had passed through the trying ordeal of public life at Washing- ton unscathed; he had climbed to a high place in the world by means which could bear a searching scrutiny. At the Chicago Convention he took no steps whatsoever to secure his own nomination as candidate for the Presidency, but was working heartily and loyally in the interest of Mr. Sherman, whom he regarded as the best candidate for the Republican party. He was a statesman, a scholar, and a gentleman. While in Congress everyone liked him, including even his strongest opponents. While bating not a jot of his principles, he was always ready to pour oil on the troubled waters of party strife, and to impart a tone of generosity into politics which is too rare, I fear, in all countries. People had looked forward too, to a happy and prosperous adminis- tration—and now all is so sadly changed. No event, how- ever, is wholly evil, and one can perceive important benefits to America and to mankind which are likely to spring from this sad tragedy. First let me say how solidly the sympathy shown by England has welded together the two ,countries which lead the civilisation of the world. Never since the obstinate folly of George 111, drove the American colonists into rebellion, has the feeling towards England been so cordial. This lam assured of by all with whom I am brought into contact. The editor of one of the leading Bos- ton papers told me that the heart of America had been touched by the genuine sympathy of Old England. He was specially pleased (and his pleasure is shared by most persons) with the letter written some weeks ago by Mr. Gladstone to Mrs. Garfield. The truly delicate tone of that letter was appreciated highly by the American people. The entente cordiale between the two countries is now complete; ald he will be an enemy of the human race who shall lift a finger to break that sacred bond of union. Another valuable result arising frOm this mournful event has been the weakening of sectional and the development of national feeling in the United States. All over this vast country, from Maine to Florida, from New York to Oregon, class, party, and local animosities and fends have been for- gotten. The nation has attained a clearer consciousness of its own being and its essential unity than ever before. It has been purified in the furnace of affliction, and has at- tained a clearer view of those great principles of humanity and justice which are to make of the American Union the beacon-light which is to lighten the world. It is remark- able that some of the warmest tributes of affectionate sor- row have come from many of those Southern States which, twenty years ago, plunged into an unrighteous war for the destruction of the Union and the maintenance of slavery. Distinctions of South and North have been forgotten in the consciousness of a common American citizenship. Speak- ing in 1863, Mr. Disraeli said: "I cannot conceal from my- self the conviction that whoever in this House may be young enough to lieie to witness the ultimate consequences of this civil war will see, whenever the waters have sub- sided, a different America from that which was known to our fathers, and even from that of which this generation has had so much experience. It will be an America of armies, of diplomacy, of rival States and menceuvring Cabinets,of fre- quent turbulence, and probably of frequent wars." Never was a prophecy so ludicrouslyabsurd read in the light of existing facts as this, and its absurdity ought to open the eyes of those) who see in Disraeli a great Statesman. He forgot the useful maxim, "Don't never prophecy unles§ you know." As a matter of fact, there is as deep, if not deeper, unity in the United States at the present mement as in any country of Europe. And it is real unity, not the monotonous uni- formity produced in the old world by a great military cen- tralising system. There is no militarism and no centrali- sation here. I have not seen a single soldier, and have only seen four policemen up to the present time in a city of four hundred thousand people. "The common sense of most" rules in America, effectively organised for national purposes in the Government at Washington. My readers may pos- sibly recollect that Chatham said he had never, in ancient or modern history, read debates so filled with the spirit of wisdom as those of the Continental Congress in Philadelphia. That great assembly " builded better than it knew." Al- though the founders of the Republic had only in view the thinly-peopled States scattered along the Atlantic sea-board, they succeeded in providing a Government which combines freedom, order, and progress for fifty millions of people over an expanse of territory as big as Europe. The excitement and suspense are now all over, and the queetion is as to President Arthur's Cabinet. Congress will not meet until December, but an executive session of the Senate will shortly be held, when Mr. Arthur will sub- mit his list for that body's approval. People are hoping for the best, but I must say that Mr. Arthur is viewed by most persons with great distrust. He was formerly collector of the Port of New York under President Grant, and owes his position to Mr. Conkling and his band of "Stalwarts." At present, however, it is not thought that Mr. Conkling will obtain Cabinet office, since such an appointment on the part of the President would render him extremely unpopular and would probably inflict serious injury on the Republican party. Mr. Arthur may be warmly attached to Mr. Conk- ling, but he cannot, it is thought, afford to flout public opinion by appointing him to high office. The danger is that the Conkling, element may work behind the scenes in the interest Of the wire-puliing faction, and to the detriment of honest administration of public affairs. People are slow to believe that Mr. Arthur's sympathies have undergone any radical change. Puck, which is the American Punch, has a coloured cartoon this week giving expression to the general sentiment. Arthur is represented as the riotous Prince Hal, now become Henry sth; Conkling is depicted as Falstaff, with Platt, as Justice Shallow, under his protection. To the solicitations of Falstaff, Arthur replies in the words of the Prince, "Presume not that I am the king I was." But underneath Puck expresses its own disbelief in Arthur's professions by entitling this scene, "A drama, which it is to be feared will not be enacted in Washington." I must say that this fear is general amongst those with whom I have coeversed. They think that the Ethiopian is Lot likely to change his skin in this way. The unpopularity of Conkling is great, though he has of course his ardent admirers, and the general opinion expressed of him is highly unfavour- able. His ambition, vanity, affected manners, and dicta- torial spirit have made him many enemies, but lie is not likely to acquiesce in his enforced retirement from public ' life, and we shall soon hear of him again on the political stage. No one can say at present how the new Cabinet will be formed, although there are many rumours. The name of Mr. Hamilton Fish is mentioned as Secretary of State. He held that Office under General Grant, and is a very wealthy and highly-respected man. Another name men- tioned is that of Dr. Andrew D. White, President of Cornell University, and late United States Minister in Berlin. Dr. White's appointment would be popular, but it is believed that he wishes to resume his duties at the University rather than enter upon an official career at Washington. Mean- while, the Conkling faction have sustained a defeat at the New York State, Republican Convention. This affords some indication of how the tide is running. The miserable wretch Guiteau now attracts some atten- tion from the public. Every morning he receives a large batch of letters by the mails. Some of these are strange documents. One writer—a lawyer—offers to defend Guiteau free of charge, since this proceeding would give him a world-wide celebrity, and consequently an influx of busi- ness. Another writer, of a very different turn of mind, draws a painful picture of the sufferings of poor Mrs. Gar- field and her children, and adds, "This is your doing, fiend! " Letters are received by the authorities of the prison suggesting plans for the torture and even burning of Guiteaa. There are thousands of men who would not hesi- tate to kill the murderer if they could get at him, and so rid the earth of se polluting a presence. A strong guard, however, is kept, and I suppose the law will take its course,

HELEN OF KIRECONNELL.—A traditionary event, whose locality is fixed in the parish of Kirkpatrick-Fleming, Dum- friesshire' is said to have given rise to this beautiful and pathetic ballad. According to the story related by Sir Walter Scott, its heroine was Helen Irving or Bell, daughter of the Laird of Kirkconnell, celebrated for her beauty, and beloved by two suitors. The favoured one was Adam Fleming, of Kirkpatrick; the name of the other is not re- corded, though his cause was espoused by the lady's friends. Helen was compelled to meet Fleming in secret, and by night, in the churchyard of Kirkconnell, a romantic spot. On one occasion the jealous lover appeared on the opposite bank of the river Kirtle, and suddenly levelled his carbine at the breast of his rival. Helen threw herself before her lover, received the bullet intended for him, and died in his arms. A mortal combat ensued between Fleming and the murderer, when the latter was cut to pieces. There are few ballads presenting such natural and simple pathos as we find here.—Cassell's Illustrated British Ballads. THE MATURE SILK WORM.—At maturity the silk worm has twelve membraneous rings or sections of its body, by which it contracts or elongates itself. It has sixteen legs, arranged in pairs—six in front, which are covered with a sort of shell or scale. The latter are placed under the first three rings, and cannot be lengthened or changed in posi- tion; the other ten are attached to the body under the rings, and are flexible, also possessing hooks by which the worm is enabled to climb in search of food. The head is enclosed in a scaly covering; the jaws are serrated, and, for the size of the insect,of great strength; its mouth is peculiar, the aper- ture being vertical instead of horizontal. On each side of the head, near the mouth, are seven very small eyes, svhilst it breathes from eighteen holes, arranged nine on each side of the body. The " spinnarets," or holes through which it draws the silken threads that make it so eminently service- able to mankind, are placed nearly close to each other, just beneath the jaw, and are exceedingly minute. The substance of which the silk is formed is a fine yellow transparet gum, secreted in two separate slender vessels, wound as it were on two spindles in the stomach; their length if unfolded would be about ten inches.—Textile Manufacturer. WHY BEES WORK MOST ice THE MORNING.—The fact that bees are most active in the morning is well established. The numbers entering the hive per minute at different hours of the day have been observed, and it is found that the greatest number are abroad in the early morning, fewest from noon onwards, whilst in the evening there is again an exodus from the hive. The result is also confirmed by the weight of the hive at different hours of the day, the weight being greater between twelve and three than at any other time, except daring the night, when all the bees are in. Laden bees returning to the hive, too, have been weighed, and M. Bonnier finds that while a bee returning from work at 9 am. weighs 1.21 gramme, or 18.67 grains, on entering the hive at 1 p.m. it only weighs 1.07 gramme, or 16.51 grains. If this difference is due merely to the early bee carrying in an additional amount of water, this would indicate his inability to distinguish between weak and strong nectar. We must therefore look for some other explanation of the greater activity of bees in the early morning than simply the greater volume of nectar in flowers at that period, and the one which roost readily suggests itself is that the num- ber of previously visited and emptied flowers must greatly increase as the day advances, owing to the number of insects abroad. The time lost in fruitless visits would consequently be greatest in the afterooon.—Good Words. HINDRANCES TO CONTENT.—One of the greatest hind- rances to content is our inability to fix the precise limit of worldly prosperity which shall make us happy. We are uncertain whether the exact sum corresponding with our idea of perfect happiness is five hundred pounds per annum or fifty thousand. The man who lives from hand to mouth sees the very El Dorado of existence in the first-named sum, while he who already enjoys it laments that it is not suffi- cient to keep up both a town and a country-house like his neighbours. Both are consequently miserable, for the spirit of thankfulness bath its abode in neither. Content is im- possible so long as there is a craving for something beyond. Strip the mask from every man we meet, and we should be filled with astonishment at the petty desires and ambitions which rule his soul. With one, the acme of social distinc- tion is to be presented at court; with another, it is obtain- ing a seat in Parliament; while a third would die happy if only he could be elected mayor of his native town; and when the honour has been obtained in each case, the re- cipient is amazed on discovering that he is not the cynosure of all evessthat in fact he remains exactly what he was before—a very ordinary personage indeed. Nay, he is more discontented than ever, for his idol has been shattered, and he has nothing to pat in its place. So, the man who is reselutely determined to have his name in the newspapers at all costs must pass through many bitter moments of humiliation, when editors take a view of his personal impor- tance essentially different from his own. These are but a few of the types of men who stand in the way of their own happiness. One has health, but covets riches; one has wealth, but would exchange it all for the rude health of the ploughboy. Money is sometimes terribly hard to carry, and could the poor but fairly assess the weight of the burden in too many instances, they might well thank God for preserv- ing them from riches. Socrates asked a questioner whether if all the men in the world should come and bring their grievances together, of body, mind, fortune, sores, ulcers, madness, epilepsies, agues, and all those common calamities of beggary, want, servitude, imprisonment, and lay them in a heap to be equally divided—would he be willing to share alike and take his portion? Without question he would prefer to remain as he was. Let the grumblers regard the matter in the same light, and there will be much less of dis- satisfaction in the world.—Good Words. Tins LESSON OF MRS. CARLYLE'S LIFE.—It might be worth our while to learn the secret of such a life; were it possible to do so, how is it that, in these latter decades of the nineteenth century, it impresses us, as we read the record of it here, like some piece of antique statuary, graceful, majestic, and yet so simply natural that it might stand as a model for countless others of the same type outwardly as its own. For we must bear in mind, indeed the value of these memorials consists largely in fact, that so far as mere outward circumstances went, Mrs. Carlyle's life differed little from that of most other women of her own rank and time. She was the wife of a distinguished roan, it is true; though when she married him be was obscure enough, and poor for years afterwards ; but for the rest, they lived and kept house together in simple, homely, and altogether ordinary fashion. Any claim to distinction which she her- self possessed rested mainly on that royalty of womanhood which the merest peasant may emulate, and which the queens of society too often lack. From the age of five-and- twenty, when she married Mr. Carlyle, her place in the world may be best defined by those two old-fashioned words, now fallen almost into desuetude, "housewife" and " help. meet"—the helpmeet of a husband who mcre than most men needed such help as she supplied.—the modest queen of a frugal home. This was the part which, for forty years, she was content to play. To perform it perfectly was the task she set herself, and with all her might accomplished. How she achieved it, and how successfully; with what fine alchemy she turned the dross of life into its gold, and made its sorriest prose take the measure of a song; and how, its the simple character of wife at home, she made her life yield for the world's good a harvest of rich increase, may be gathered from these brief but graphic records, which every woman who has a home to guide, or a life other than her own to share, may study to advantage.—Good Words. THE LIBERATION SocirrY.—The Executive Committee of this body have just issued a circular to their supporters, acquainting them with their plan of operations during the approaching season. The change which has taken place in the position of ptiblic affairs enables them to again wigoronsly press the question of disestablishment; that it may take a prominent place among the questions to be dealt with by Parliament and the constituencies. Accordingly, Mr. Peddie, M.P., will next session submit a moticn in favour of the disestablishment of the Scotch Church, which will be sustained by outdoor action, both in Scotland and England, Events in the English Church are, it is alleged, rapidly preparing the way for its disestablishment also, and these, with proposals for organic change, afford opportunities for educating the public mind which will be diligently used. The ettinctien of the remaining State-grants for ecblesiastical purposes in the colonies will be sought. The Government is to be urged to prepare a measure for bringing the Burial AZts into harmony with the Act of last session, and thereby "finally to close a controversy which no one can wish to prolong.' The principal religious equality may, it is stated, need to be asserted in connection with the new statutes for the colleges of Oxford and Cambridge, and with new educational legislation for Wales, and it is intended to co-operate with those who are seeking for the abolition of ecclesiastical tests in denominational colleges which are mainly supported by public funds. Some special questions in the Metropolis relating to charities, churches, and ecclesiastical exaction are to be dealt with, and there is to be an increase in the number of the Society's meetings, 'lectures, and publications, which will afford detailed informa- tion relative to the several topics named in the 'circular. BARROW-IN-FURNESS, Monday.—There was a fair atten- dance on 'Change this morning, and although the business actually done was inconsiderable, a good tone was noted in connection with the various departments of industry in the. district. Pig iron is selling in very heavy parcels, and deliveries continue very large. Two furnaces have been blown in during the week, and it is evident the increased output will be required to meet the demands made upon makers who are likely, from present appearances, to no fully employed during the winter months. Prices are un: disturbed-625. Gd. for No. 1 Bessemer end 60s. for No. 3 forge at works. Stocks have been further reduced. Steel makers are very fully employed in all departments, and prices are firmer. LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAY.—During the last for all considerable anxiety has been manifest in the coal trade o. this district as to the course of events as regards prices and wages at the close of the month. The tendency a the market is certainly towards an advance. All classes of round coal continue in good, steady demand, and the only descrip- tion of fuel with which colliery proprietors experience difficulty at present is slack, which, although in very 'al, demand, has, owing to the largely increased productionnam late, overtaken the requirements of consumers, and at 50.4 collieries considerable stocks are being put down. 'What appears to be an agrarian murder is reported to have been committed in county Clare. On Saturday evening a tenant farmer named Michael Moloney, living at Rath- clooney, near Ennis, was sitting in his parlour when two shots were fired through the window, killing him on the spot. His wife had a narrow escape, the shots grazing her face. It is stated that the deceased had been on bad terms with his neighbours, and on Sunday morning a threatening notice was found posted on his gate. No arrests have been made. The police attended at the rooms of the Cork Branch of the Land League on Saturday forenoon to give effect to the proclamation of the Lord-Lieutenant. Those who had been in the habit of attending the weekly meetings on Saturday assembled, but the police informed them that any meeting attempted would be dispersed, and though several persons showed an inclination to defy lawful authority the leaders announced that no meeting would be held—that, in fact, the Land League had ceased to exist. After the crowd had separated the principal members of the League met privately, and a correspondent says that there is little doubt that a plan was arranged for carrying on in secret the work of the Proscribed society. That open resistance to the proclama- tion is abandoned is manifest from the fact that no repre- sentative of the League attended an execution sale held in the Cork Court House. In the Dublin City Council, on Tuesday, Mr. Gray, M.P., moved that the honorary freedom of the city should be con- ferred upon Messrs. Parnell and Dillon. A. special meeting of the Council had been called to consider the proposal, and the hall was packed with people, who were demonstrative in their approval of Mr. Gray's speech, in which the opinion was expre9sed by the hon. gentleman that Mr. Parnell was imprisoned because he had worsted Mr. Gladstone in argu- ment, and Mr. Dillon because he had repudiated with scorn the compliments paid him by the Premier. Mr. Maurice Brooks, M.P., for Dublin, led the opposition to Mr. Gray's proposal, desiring to show that the Dublin Municipal Council did not approve of the Land League. A reference by a member to Archbishop Croke as "the Rock of Cashel" was received with laughter and hisses. On a division there voted for Mr. Gray's motion 23 members and against it the same number, and it was rejected by the casting vote of the Lord Mayor. Now that the Land League is quelled there are indications that Irsh farmers are disposed and even happy to turn their backs upon it. A remarkable meeting of County Wicklow tenants has been convened by Mr. Fitzwilliam Dick. That venerable and respected landlord, as well as the Earl of, Wicklow, the Hon. Mr. Fitzwilliam, and other gentlemen, advised a loyal adherence to law and order, and the speeches were frequently applauded. Mr. Fitzwilliam (son of Earl Fitzwilliam) said that since he had come over from England be had found that there were in Irelund a far greater number of. persons ready to support Her Majesty than he had any idea of. Mr. Fitzwilliam appears to have struck a responsive chord when he expressed his belief that there were many good loyal men and true all over the country, who only wanted leaders to unite them in a great and powerful organisation to make a stand against the aggression of the Land League. The meeting was most enthusiastic through- out, mad it adopted unanimously a number of resolutions rejectineb the teachings of the Land League, approving the so-called-coercive action of the Government, and declaring a determination to uphold the constitution and the laws of the country. There are reports from various parts of Ire- land of tenants in large numbers taking the preliminary steps towards their appearance before the new Land Court. The farmers on an estate near Ballincollig, county Cork, who were about to pay their rents were visited on Wednes- day night by a party of intimidators, and Michael Walsh, one of the tenants, was shot in the groin. A large number of arrests under the provisions of the Protection Act was made on Monday. Dr. Kenny, of Dublin, who has been in attendance professionally on Mr. Parnell, Mr. Dillon, and others in Kilmainham Gaol, and who was himself treasurer of the Land League, was arrested on Monday. In the latest batch of ' suspects " is a Miss Ilodnett, of Ballydehob, Kerry, who had exhibited the Land League's manifesto from the window of her house. The arrest of Miss Hodnett may have some influence on the fortunes of the Ladies' Land League. It is stated that the Prisons Board have held an inquiry at Kilmainham Gaol as to how the signatures to the "No Rent" manifesto were rib- tamed, and that Messrs. Parnell, Kettle, Dillon, and Brennan refused to answer the questions put to them, for which Mr. Forster ordered that they should be deprived of all visits and communications for seven days. Mr. Parnell was, how- ever," interviewed " lately in Kilmainham Gaol. He is said to have declared his belief that the farmers would to a great extent refuse to pay rent, and t -i have remarked that by their teceut use of the Protection Act the Government had prac- tically rendered it impossible for the farmers either to test or safely use the Land Act. Reports of the breaking up of branches of the League come from various quarters. In this connection it is of interest to note that the farmers on Major Bourke's estate at Iristdown, where the first of the League's "missionary "meetings was held, have been the first in the Tuam district to pay their rents. Some of the Irish leaders in the United States are urging that the Land League head-quarters should be transferred to New York. Telegrams sent to the officers of the League have not been replied to, and the Irish-Americans have come to the con- elusion that the British Government has prevented the delivery of the messages. Within the last two or three days there has been a noticeable diminution in the Ameri- can collections for the purposes of the League. , THE LAND ACT IN OPERATION. Hundreds of tenant farmers marched into Timm on Wed- nesday to get notices filled up with regard to the readjust- ment of rent under the Land Act. So great was the demand for papers that the local stamp distributor had to telegraph for more. Cheers were given for the Land Act, and a general desire evinced to avail themselves of its provisions.
