div.p: bARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
THE EX,',IIINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1881.
NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.

The annual meeting of the National Lihrral Federation was held on Tuesday, in Liverpool, under the presidency of Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P. About 200 gentlemen, represent- ing Liberal associations in different parts of the country, were present. Among whom were the followimg :—War- rington, Mr. W. Long, Mr. J. H. Gornall, Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., Messrs. F. A. Roberts, C. S. Burgess, F. Dixon, J. Harrison, T. Davie, W. Wright, J. Mounfield, J. Green, H Roberts, J. Craik, and S. Jones. Rev. A. Kenworthy, Messrs' C. J. Holmes, W. Brome, G. Halford, and A. H. Dun.—Mr. GOLDWIN SMITH, who had been invited but was unable to attend, wrote a letter in which, referring to the condition of Ireland, he said:—" All Liberals must deplore the necessity for the arrests. But so, we may be sure, does a Government the head of which is Mr. Gladstone, and among the members of which are Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain. The power exercised by the Ministry cannot be called unconstitutional, since it was constitutionally entrusted to them by Parlia- ment to meet an emergency which has unquestionably arisen. The ultimate aim of the persons who had been arrested was not justice to the Irish farmer. It was the same as that of the Fenian organisation in the United States from which their funds are derived, and which has twice invaded Canada for the purpose of kindling civil war. Let civil war break out, and we shall have the whole circle of Irish calamities over again." The annual report of the Council was an interestiN docu- ment, referring to the leading political topics which occupied Parliament during the late Session. The Irish Land Act leaving practically monopolised the whole atten- tion of the Legislature, it was pointed out that the reforms urged last year upon the Ministers have still to be under- taken, and a hope was expressed that in the course of next Session some of them will be introduced and carried into law. Reference was made to the much-discussed circular issued by the Federation inviting the constituencies to bring legitimate pressure to bear upon those Liberal repre- sentatives who endeavoured to oppose certain vital princi- ples of the Land Bill when the measure was before the House of Commons. The circular in question was criticised at the time as an attempted interference with members' freedom of action; but the Federation Committee point out, in justifying their conduct, that the document in question was urgently needed, and that it exercised a salutary effect. During the year a considerable number of new associations had been admitted into the Federation, including several county associations. The report was adopted, and resolutions were passed demanding immediate reform of the English land laws, and an extension of the county franchise.

Board of Trade having been enthusiastically received, the right li,nouratito gentleman addressed, the company at con- siderable lenglith, Lis speech including references to the questions of free trade, fair trade, the treaty negotiations with. France, obstruction in,the House of Commons, the attitude of the Oonservative party, the convention with the Boers, our relations with the United States, and the grow- ing prosperity of England.

ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE. The annual meeting of this society was held on Tuesday in the Assembly Room, Brook-street. The Rev. R. J. Ward, president of the society, occupied the chair, and there were about 200 persons present. The chairman said they had occasion to be thankful for what the society had done in the past, and they could look hopefully for its future welfare. The temperance movement was making progress in the , country. Speaking of the Sunday closing movement, he I said this was the first time they had held a public meeting in connection with the Band of Hope since the passing of the Act compelling the publichouses in Wales to be closed on Sundays. He thought they would all be glad that such a measure had been passed, altholigh it had not come into operation so quickly. The passing of the Act was a good thing for Wales, and if it was good for that part of the king- dom, why should not a similar measure be good for England? Their society was in a healthy condition, and he was proud to be its president. The members associated with the society were working very heartily for the cause of temperance, and he hoped their numbers would further increase, and that their mark would be more successful in the future than it had been in the past. He firmly believed that no Sunday school was complete unless it had a Band of Hope connected with it. They had the sympathy of those who were eugaged in the Sunday school, an he was glad to see that their society was so closely united with it. He would like to see the number of members attending the weekly meetings increasing. The average attendance during tte winter they had just entered upon was 60 out of a roll of 350, which was not what it ought to be. He was sure all who attended the meetings could not fail to derive pleasure and profit. There were recitations given which were a source of enjoyment to those who listened to them, and which would prove advan- tageous to those who learned them. He counselled the younger members of the society to keep to thei. promises and to have nothing to do with strong drink. In Ireland they had been trying to put a placard out which said "No , rent," but this was not allowed. Their society had also a I placard which said "No drink," but they were allowed to carry on their good work. (Applause.) He requested the parents to let their childien attend the meetings which would tend to their moral and spiritual welfare. The following report was then read and adopted, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Joshua Boydell :—The time has again come round when your committee have to meet with the members of the society to lay before you the report of their proceed- ings during the eight months they had been in office, and also to resign into your hands the trust which you com- mitted to their care. From various causes we regret to report that the number of public meetings has not been so large as we could have desired, there being only one which was very successful in every respect. But we considered our chief duty lay not so much in getting up public meet- ings as in laying hold of the young, and with that end in view arrangements were made at the beginning of the year for a meeting of the members to be held every week which consisted of singing and recitations by members of the com- mittee and friends. From January to the end of May 16 meetings were held with an average attendance of 45; and although this may appear a small attendance, we believe these meetings have been productive of much good by the evils of intemperance being constantly brought before the notice of the members and training them up into habits of sobriety and truth. Although see have only been able to hold one public meeting in connection with our own Band of Hope, our choir has not been idle, for under the conductor- ship of Mr. A. E. West they have given successful enter- tainments in connection with the Band of Hope at Parr Stocks, Pearley Cross, and Gerard's Bridge. We deeply regret that we cannot retain the services of Mr. West, who has been compelled throggh a great pressure of other duties to give up his office as conductor of the choir; and the committee take this opportunity of thanking him for kis ser- vices in the past; at the same time we congratulate ourselves on having secured the services of Mr. Elliott. On Whit- Monday 300 of our members took part in the annual demon- stration of the St. Helens Band of Hope Union, which the young people thoroughly enjoyed, considering the great number of people there was on the ground. We are glad to report a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £2 15s. 4d., which will be of great service to the committee in the work they have undertaken during the coming winter, and we trust that the arrangements made for the members meet- ings will conduce to the moral and spiritual welfare of the members. During the past eight months 24 new members have joined the society, which brings the total number of names on the pledge book up to 362, all of whom we believe to be thorough abstainers, as the pledge book has recently been thoroughly revised. We desire to return our warmest thanks to those kind friends who have from time to time cordially responded to our appeals; to our pastor, superintendents, and teachers of the school for the sympathy and help manifested towards us, and believe that in proportion as the great importance of the temperance movement, especially amongst the young, is seen and felt by them, so shall we gain more and more of their goodwill, support, and co-operation, and at the same time we would ever look above for the approval of God whose Well done' is of far greater value than the praise of man." The following officers were elected :—President, Rev. R. J. Ward; vice-presidents, Messrs. C. Sharpies and Joshua Boy- den ; treasurer, Mr. John Moss; conductor of choir, Mr. J. T. Elliott; hon. sec.. Mr. James Robertshaw ; committee, Miss Thompson, Miss A. F. Sharpres, Messrs. Charles Barker, James McCall, Charles Hodgetts, Thomas Stevens, John Wildman, J. Sharpies, J. Burchall, Harry Berry, J. C. Westworth, and Mr. Buckley. The Rev. J. W. Walker, 8.A., of Huyton, also addressed the meeting. Songs were given by M. Elliott, Miss Sharpies, Mr. P. Richardson; part songs and glees by the Albion Glee Union; a violin solo by Mr. Harry Berry; and recitations by Messrs. A. Lucas, J. Wardleworth, J. W. Gray, and Chas. Hodgetts.
DINNER TO CANVASSERS AT
ST. HELENS.

On Tuesday night, Dr. Jamison, the newly-elected town councillor for Hardshaw Ward, entertained his canvassers and friends at dinner in the Assembly Room of the Fleece Hotel. Dr. Jamison occupied the chair, and Dr. Twyford the vice-chair. The following gentlemen sat at the table—. Messrs. Josias C. Gamble, Massey, T. Cook, S. Wolfenden, Duffy, Dromgoole, W. G. Ashton, Joseph Ogden, A. C Clarke, Joshua Boyden, C. Thornton, A. F. Muir, Apple- ton, Henry Ashton, Derbyshire, W. Middlehurst, William Battersby, genry Galton, Thomas Riley, William Twist, William H. K. Kitchen, John Donnelly, Rosser, J. Hough- ton, George Clarke, H. Caine, John Taylor, and Morris.
The CitaticuAN proposed "The Queen and the Royal Family," and "The Army, Navy, and Volunteers," which were duly honoured, Captain DUFFY reponding to the latter toast.

Dr. TWYFORD said that the toast he was about to propose would, he was sure, be received particularly well by every- one present in that room, and that was the health of their new town councillor. (Applause.) He could assure them he felt very proud that Dr. Jamison had been induced to give a considerable portion of his time to the work of the town, and he congratulated him upon having done so. He felt that Dr. Jamison would be an acquisition to the Council —(applause)—as he would then endeavour to improve the state of the atmosphere of St. Helens, because he resided in St. Helens and knew how fleeces try it was to have pure air. He felt sure that in the Council Dr. Jamison would do his best to carry out those views, of which he had given expres- sion outside, and he was sure he would touch such an itn- portant subject with prudence, caution, and care. There was no doubt that the manufactures in St. Helens were very important, and they needed to be very cautious with regard to anything that would tend to interfere with the manufac- turers in any way, but he had no doubt Dr. Jamison would do his best to clear away the nuisances of which there were now great complaints. He had known Dr. Jamison for about 17 years, and during that time it had been a pleasure and a privilege to know him—(applause)—and if he served the town in the same way that he had served the firm, be would serve it well indeed. (Applause.) He was sure they would drink hishealth heartily. The toast was honoured with loud cheers for Dr. Jamison and family. Dr. Jamrsoze, responding, said that when he first came to St. Helens it ought to liave been a bright and clear day, and it might have been, but it certainly did not appear so. (Laughter.) And when he walked up Church-street and looked round he thought it was the dirtiest place he had ever been in, and the sooner he got out of it the better. He had not, however, been long in St. Helens before he altered his mind about getting out of it, and he staved there, and the reason was because he met so good a man as Dr. Twy- ford, whose friendship it was a pleasure and a profit to possess, and during the 17 years his friendship and inter- course had been almost the chief charm and pleasure in St. Helens. (Applause.) During all those years one would naturally become identified with the place, and he had always taken a great pride in the industry of the St. Helens people, and whilst he had done so he had rather re gretted that St. Helens had taken the motto which said that its light was got from the earth. He should have thought that they would have preferred getting it from above, but it appeared that they thought light was only to be extracted from below. (Laughter.) Taking a pride in St. Helens because It represented the vigour and industry of the age as manifested by applied science, he had really been angry and irritited beyond measure to hear it called "a hell hole ;" and angry that the eldest son of the chief secretary for Ire- land, in discussing civilisation in England, put the question whether civilisation was worth having if such places as St. Helens were permitted to exist. When young Mr. Forster said that he felt angry beyond measure, and thought that some pride should be taken in th 4 place to make it less re- pulsive to outsiders. They existed by the trade and the peculiarites of the place which were not of too savoury a nature, and whatever measures should be taken or striven to be taken to make the place better, the manufactures and industries ought not to suffer loss, but rather be cultivated. To bring manufactures to St. Helens nothing would give him greater pleasure to see, and to have the furnaces in use as hard as they could, but with as little nuisance as they could. (Applause.) In St. Helens there were a hard-work- ing and laborious Reople.. A woman in Rigby-street once said to him when he saw her husband asleep, "I feel sorry for him; it's all work and bed." The man was a collier and got up at four in the morning, and in coming home at night went to bed. When one considered the laboriousness of the work, and how hard and cheerless it was, whatever they could do to make it more pleasant and more happy for those engaged in the work, it was their bounden duty to do it. (Applause.) Manufacturers had many duties—not only profit and loss duties, but others to the public. Although they had done something they had not done as much as they might have done. If the manufacturers had done more than they had that of which they complained would not have got to be of so serious a character as it now as- sumed. He should endeavour as far as he could in the Council to make the town better to live in—having due regard to whatever interests there were—and more pleasant and cheerful in order that they might take a pride in it. Every man ought to have a feeling of pride in the town in which he lived. St. Helens manufacturers made their money in the town and lived elsewhere, and St. Helens was handed over to horrible smells, so that the outsiders won- dered how they lived there. With those feelings to which he had given expression be should go into the Council and try to make the place much better than it was. I ME. S. WOLFENDEN proposed "The town and trade of St. Helens." He said they had heard what their new coun- cillor and also the chairman of the Health Committee had said about not hampering the trades of the &Ism, but at the same time to make the town as pleasant as possible. Such gentlemen as Drs. Twyford and Jamison they needed, and ought to have in the Council Chamber, so that trade might progress in a manner satisfactory to them all. They had it on the authority of the late mayor that the the trade of St. Helens was likely to progress. The trade of the town was pretty well divided, and when one trade was not perhaps what it might be other things kept the town going until that revived. They also had it on the authority of their future mayor that the trade bad begun to revive. (Hear, bear.) He was pleased to hear that, and every one connected with the town would be equally pleased at the announcement. (Applause.) He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. J. C. Gamble.

Mr. Jonas C. GAMBLE, in responding, said he was informed the other day that the engineering trade was improving,and he was glad to hear it, but he was sorry to say other trades were not improving at present, at least he did not see many signs of it. Their chairman and host seemed in his address the other day to be rather making an attack on the trade of St. Helens, but he was glad to hear that he was doing the 'same as other people who became responsible for their utter- ances, and was now modifying them. (Laughter and "N0,n0.") He quite agreed with everything Dr. Jamison had said that night, by which they could see a considerable modification of his expressions—(" No, no,")—and he agreed that every- thing sh6uld be done to improve the state of the atmosphere of St. Helens, without injuring or hampering its trade. He, himself, lived in the town, and perhaps, suffered with others through the defects of the atmosphere, and he was quite willing that everything should be done to improve it. He hoped that Dr. Jamison would findlmeans to carry out his ideas, but with a little caution and prudence,—as the vice- chairman had said,—and going about it in a right way he might succeed. (Applause.) Mr. DROMGOOLE proposed the health of the Town Council. In all regulated societies they had to give a certain amount of latitude and power into the hands of a number of their citizens for the purpose of governing the town. In some towns that power was not delegated into right hand., but in St. Helens their efforts had been successful in selecting the best men to govern the town. Of course, there would boa few odd mere outside anxious to get in. He hoped to see some Alteration shortly by which additional members would be returned from each ward to the town Council. In 1869, perhaps 24 members were quite sufficient, but since that time there had been a material increase in the population of the town. Referring to their past mayors, the list, from Mr. Gamble to begin with, to Mr. Harrison, their present retir- ing mayor, would compare favourably with any town, both as regarded the intelligence and the diligence with which they discharged their duties. Their aldermen had won their position by hard work, and good service to the town. The Health Committee was one of the most important of the committees, and that was presided over by Dr. Twyford. After referring to other committees, the speaker referred to the water supply, and said that when they got an additional supply lie hoped the water rates for domestic supply would not be increased. Perhaps the manufacturers would not ob- ject to having their rates a little bit advanced, and although he objected to taxes upon trade, still water was a raw material, and they would have to bear the rise in the market the same as other materials. He coupled with the toast the names of Mr. Thomas Cook and Mr. Joseph Massey. (Ap- plause.) I Mr. Councillor Coox regretted they had not an alderman present to respond to that toast. The toast was of so im- portant a nature that they ought to have had, an alderman. [The CHAIRMAN: But we have not any turtle. (Laughter.)] He supposed the Town Council of St. Helens were regarded as a necessary evil, and he was afraid they sometimas re- ceived more kicks than thanks. He would tell them can- didly that the Town Council of St. Helens were entitled to the thanks of the community instead of kicks. They did their duty faithfully and diligently to the beet of their ability. He did not mean to say that they were infallible, or that they never made mistakes, because no human institu- tion was infallible or was free from mistakes. Certain duties devolved upon them, and they tried to perform those duties conscientiously. They tried to keep the rates within reasonable bound, but they aimed at efficiency first. He agreed that the representation of the town was not wide enough, because it was very hard work for 24 men to do the work required to be done. About half a dozen really worked very little, so that 18 or 20 members had to do all the work in their respective committees, for the work of the Council was simply to confirm what was done in those committees In his own case he found that since November he had attended 12$ meetings. It was too much for any man— (hear, hear)—it was too much to expect from any man unless he was a gentleman free from business. The Town Council bad done a great deal of work within the last ten years, but sill there remained a good deal to be done, and he congratu- lated the town upon having secured so efficient a member as Dr. Jamison. (Applause.) They wanted men of education and practical knowledge to help them in carrying the work on. He thought it was quite right that their attention s should be turned to the smoke nuisance but it must be re- membered that all improvement in art and science was a

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON THE IRISH CRISIS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON THE IRISH CRISIS.

In the evening a great Liberal meeting was held in Hengler's Circus, and was attended by the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P. The building, which will hold about 5,000 persons, was densely crowded. Mr. R. D. Holt, president of the Liverpool Liberal Association, occupied the chair, and was supported by Lord Houghton Mr. Serjeant Simon, M.P., Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., Mr. g. Williamson, M.P., Mr. Ashton Dilke, M.P., Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. Waugh, M.P., Mr. Borlass, M.P., Mr. E. Williams, M.P., Mr. A. H. Brown, M.P., Mr. Joseph Arch, Mr, H. Yates Thompson Sir J. J. Picton, Mr. Schnadhorst, Mr. A. G. Symonds (National Reform Union), the Rev. J. Freeston, and many others. The CHAIRMAN gave a cordial welcome to Mr. Chamber- lain, and went on to express great regret that the Irish electors in Liverpool should have decided to desert the Liberal party and vote for the Tories in the coming muni- cipal elections. The course adopted by the Government in the present crisis, however much on some grounds it was to be regretted, was justifiable. (Loud cheers.) Their attend- ance that night in such large numbers showed that at least in the hearts of Liverpool Liberals confidence 'in the leaders of the nation's policy had not been imperilled or impaired. (Loud cheers). Mr. H. F. PEASE moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting hereby expresses its thorough confidence in her Majesty's Ministers, trusting to their ability to effect much needed reforms, and to their determination to main- tain the unity, the honour, and the liberties of the nation." (Cheers). Mr. Was. CROSFIELD seconded the resolution, which was carried with acclamation. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in rising to acknowledge the resolu- tion, was received with enthusiastic cheers and the singing of "He's a jolly good fellow." He said : When some time ago I received the invitation of the National Federation to take part in this meeting, I thought that itomight very likely be my duty to address to you something like a general survey of the whole policy of the Government. (Hear, hear.) No doubt there have recently been accomplished events of the. greatest importance in Afghanistan, in Africa, and in Europe, which, on ordinary occasions would com- mand your serious attention. I thought, too, that I might possibly direct attention to some of those great questions of domestic legislation to which Mr. Crosfield has just referred, which ought to have a large place in the programme of any Liberal Government. Some of those unsolved problems, the arrears of a long period of Tory rule' and especially some of those subjeGts which have been brought recently into prominence by the depression in trade, which is now hap- pily passing away. But under the circumstances in which we meet to-night, I have thought that I should better con- sult your wishes and inclinations if I left these matters to other speakers, or to a future time, because although they are of great intrinsic importance, I think they yield in im- mediate interest to that great subject which is now filling all our minds with grave solicitude and anxious expectation. Mr. Chairman, I hope I may take the cordiality with which the resolution you have put from the chair has just been carried, and the presence in such vast numbers of this great audience here to-night as indications that the Liberals of Liverpool and the representatives of Liberal- ism gathered here from so many neighbouring places are prepared to support the Government—(loud cheers)— in the measures which they have deemed it necessary to take in the interests of public safety in Ireland. If I were addressing an audience of ,Conservatives should expect at least as much as this—(hear, hear), but from you, gentlemen, before I sit down, I shall nenture to ask for more. (Hear, hear.) I ask from you not only a patriotic acquiescence in a pressing necessity, before which party spirit is silent, and party rancour itself stands ashamed—(cheers), but I ask you to go with me in an ex- amination of what has happened before, of what has still to come, and to consider the whole course and policy of the Government of which the present situation is only one, and a very partial, manifestation. (Hear, hear.) I read in an article in a Tory newspaper that the recent action of the Government is to be considered as a triumph of sound Con- servative doctrines—(laughter)—over Radical theories in the Cabinet. (Laughter.) Well, I need only say to you that if that were the case I don't think I should to-night have the honour of addressing you as a member of Her Majesty's Government. (Cheers.) Our political opponents are in too great haste to be glad. (Hear, hear.) There is one cardinal distinction between them and us to which I should like to call your attention at the outset. With them coercion is a policy—(loud cheers); they have no other. With us it is only a hateful incident. (Renewed cheers.) We have arrived at a point at which the two opinions meet, but we have travelled along very different roads, and I hope we shall soon part company again. (Loud cheers.) For the moment we stand shoulder to shoulder to resist any danger—(hear, hear) ; but we differ altogether as to the past and future means of prevention and of cure. (Oheers.) We, Liberal and Radical, are alike prepared, if the necessity arises, to put down rebellion— (cheers)—but we do not quarel with reform. (Hear.) Sup- pression of disorder is, I think Mr. Pease told us, the first duty of a Government. Ido not say that, but I say that it is an urgent and sacred duty, and I know no Liberal or Radical who will venture to dispute it. (Hear, bear.) Law is the guarantee of liberty, and it appears to me, therefore, that there may be times when it is the highest duty of a Liberal to support and assert the law. (Hear, hear.) On the other hand, there is another duty which I regard as at least as urgent, and even more sacred, and that is to search out the cause of the disorder—(hear, hear)—and, where possible, remove it. (Cheers.) Well, now, it is because the Government have performed this other, and, in my opinion, this greater duty, that we find our quarrel just, that I am entitled to stand before you to-night to challenge your judgment and hold myself permitted to defend the law— (hear)—which I and my colleagues have done our best to purge from oppression and from wrong. (Loud cheers.) Thus, Mr. Chairman, you will see that in the judgment which you are called upon to give time is an essential element in tho question. I have to show you, if I may, that we have not acted either too soon or too late. "(Hear, hear.) If we have delayed too long I admit we have made an error which may be fatal. If we have acted too soon we have committed what Ido not hesitate to say is a political crime. I think you will see that I have endeavoured to put before you a plain issue, and that I don't shirk the responsibility which rests upon every member of the Govgrnment, and upon everybody St ho pre- tends to support them. (Applause.) Now, in meet- ing charges which are made against us from opposite quarters I shall have to ask you to bear with me while I once more, for I know not how many times, go over the con- ditions of this hard problem, with which we have to deal. It is not a new problem this Irish question. Once in. ten years, once in twenty years it may be, sometimes with sufficient warning, sometimes without the slightest prepara- tion, like a bolt from the blue, the Irish question is upon us. Every generation in turn for four hundred years has had to deal with it. (Hear, hear.) Each has disposed of it for the time according to its fashion, and each has had to bequeath it still unsettled to its successor. It is all very well for Lord Salisbury—(hisses)—with that historical accuracy for which he is famous—(laughter)—to pretend that the present situation is the fault of Mr. Gladstone or of Mr. Gladstone's Ministry. Lord Salisbury's memory is notorious. (Laughter.) He cannot recollect the plain terms of a public document to which he has set his hand a few weeks before. (Renewed laughter.) How is it to be expected that he should remember facts of Irish history. (Hear hear.) But we knew that for the whole time to which' he referred the Irish people have been constantly dissatisfied. There has not been, lam afraid, one single year during which the removal of the English garrison would not have been the signal for an instant uprising of ' the people, and a declaration of their independence. On Wednesday, Mr. Chamberlain was entertained at a banquet by the members of the Liverpool Reform Club. Mr. T. Brocklebank, jun. chairman of the club, presided. Lord Houghton and Mr. liathbone, M.P., responded to the toasts of the Houses of Parliament. The health of the President of the

Mr. Chamberlain, replying to a correspondent, says it is impossible to say whether the Bankruptcy Bill will pass the House of Commons next session, but it is certainly his in- tention to introduce it at the earliest opportunity. On Wednesday, Sir William Harcourt received deputa- tions from various public bodies in Glasgow, and at an informal reception at night the executive of the Glasgow Liberal Association presented the Home Secretary with an address, to which he delivered a brief reply. TIIE BEAR AND TILE PANTIIER.—A hunter in North America once witnessed a terrific combat between a bear and a panther. He had thrown himself down by a forest lake to rest after the labours of the day, when he was suddenly aroused by the most horrible howling. Presently a bear emerged from the wood, looking for a way of escape, but finding none. Shortly afterwards a panther appeared, which at once attacked the bear, springing upon its back and assailing it in the fiercest manner. The two animals fought with the utmost fury for a considerable time: but at last the bear fell dead. As soon as the struggle was ended the panther went to the lake to quench its thirst, and on its return a well-directed bullet from the spectator of the fight laid it low.—From" Little Folks Magazine" for October. Cnntors ELonamENT.—A heartless elopement has occurred at Balloch, in Scotland. A young man, a brick- layer, was engaged to get married to the younger of two sisters, who resided with their parents at Dalvait, near Bal- loch. The customary proclamation of banns had been posted up by the registrar at Jamestown, and the marriage was to have taken place this week. On Friday night, while a few of the friends of the betrothed couple were enjoying them- selves at the residence of the bride, the young man, wishing to have some talk with his intended wife, asked her to step outside. After talking for some time, be requested her to return to the house as the night was intensely cold, and he would follow immediately. The young man did not return in a reasonable time, however, and on investigation being made it was discovered that while the conversation at the door had been takipg place the elder sister had retired to another room, where she had collected her sister's "braws," and with them escaped by a back window, the bridlayer being ready, not far off, to receive her. The pair have not since been heard of.

WARM-TIC AND Cos.—lf we considerhewmuch less closely the round threads of wool or silk can lie together than the flat fibres of flax or cotton, we can readily under- stand why the absorptive powers of the latter are so much inferior to those of wool, the matted threads of which can take up and retain by cappillary attraction a wonderfully large amount of water. But in addition to these many excellencies, the value of wool, especially for underclothing, is still further enhanced by the healthy friction which it exercis,s on the skin, helping to remove or brush away ex- creted matter, which might otherwise accumulate and seriously obstruct the pores, and this it does doubtless in virtue of these scales or imbrications, microscopic though they be. There is thus every reason for urging that woollen garments, thick or thin according to the season, should constantly be worn next to the skin, for although silk is no doubt almost as suitable for underclothing, owing to its much greater cost it can never come in general use for such pur- poses.—Pront article by a Government Analyst in " Cassell's Family Magazine" for October. ji'HEN Is no BATH SAM—There are few greater ad- mirers of the bath than I myself am. I like almost every plan of bathing—with the exception, probably, of the Russian moudjilc plan of getting in under the stove, and burying yourself in hot ashes. I have never tried that, but doubtless it has its advantages—to a moudjik. However, I must say there is such a thing as over-doing even the bath. Although I should wish that every one in this country were like myself—amphibious, so that if thrown into the water he would only ponder, while quietly swimming out again, where the nearest place was at which to procure dry clothes and a cup of coffee, still it must be remembered that men are not manatees. We could not live most of our time in the water, like those interesting aquatic mammals.. People shoult neither bathe too often in the day, nor remain too lonelli the water at a time, else they will over-do it, they will have too much of a good thing. The after-effects of the bath should in all cases be studied, as well as the state of the general health. Moreover, the temperature of the water deserves Consideration, it may suit some people to break the ice on their matntinal tub in winter, with a frozen sponge for a mallet, but a dash of warm water is to be re- commeded when themercury crosses the line 32 dega. One bath in winter, and two in the heat of summer, I would call not over-doing the thing.—The Family Doctor in " Cassell's Magazine" for October.

St. Helens had not done badly for Dr. Jamison, and there was a great contrast between Dr. Jamison of to-day and of the same gentleman some years ago, when he used to think how much Dr.. Jamison wanted some flesh on his bones. (Laughter.) But the town had well arranged streets, which were well sewered, and the brook was now nearly free from acidity. The Gas Committee of which he was proud to be the chairman had done its duty well. The gas, which was as good as any in England with, perhaps, the exception of Carlisle, had been reduced from 33. 9. per thousand cubic feet to 3s. 4d. at different times which re- presented a saving to gas consumers of £4,200 a year. That department he considered was very economically managed, and over £l,lOO were handed over to the Borough Fund a short time ago. Referring to the water questions he said that he found that the quantity of water used by manufacturers was equal to that used for domestic purposes, so that they were on a fair and equitable basis. They had found that a supply of water could be obtained cheaper than from the Liverpool Corporation, and as prudent men they were taking the wisest step in going elsewhere. and this had the recom- mendation of Major Tullock, one of Her Majesty's iospectors. IThe Primitive Methodists of I:Ugh-street Chapel, Over, had the benefit of a lecture by the Rev. J. Ferguson, of Old Hill, on behalf of the Sunday school. The subject was "The life of Gladstone?' The lecturer was introduced by Mr. J. Tomkinson, J.P., of Willington Hall, who very suitably spoke of the great man as one who is an ardent admirer and a wil'ing follower. The lecturer, who was well received, eloqueli,:s set before the audience a succinct ac- count of the Prem:er as the son of Sir John Gladstone. born iat Liverpool 180, educated at Eton and Oxford, where he stood well till 1331, when be went on a Continental tour. Then he put up for Newark as a Conservative and became I in 1831 under secretary for the colonies in Sir 'Robert Peel's ;Ministry. In 1841 he was made vice-president and in 1843 president for the Board of Trade. In the general election in • 1847 he became M.P. for Oxford, and in 1852 he was chosen . Chancellor for the Aberdeen ministry, which he held for three years. Lord Palmerston's ministry made him Chan- cellor, and when Mr. Disraeli resigned in 1898 he became Premier, and passed the Act for Abolition of the Irish , Church. the Irish Tenant Right Bill, the Peace Preservation Act, and again in 1879, till now be has been to the fore passing the Irish Land Bill, the worth of which he is now i proving. He showed that Mr. Gladstone is not unworthy of . the position he holds In a literary point of view. At various • times he has proved that his pen is a power in England as . well as his elognence. Such will be seen by a perusal of his "State in relation to the Church," "Church princi- ples tracedgo their results," essays on a multitude of sub- jects, and last but not least in his translation of Homer. r Altogether he is a man of whom England is justly proud.

div.p: meat in past times has not been lightly dwelt upon, with the assurance that "we shall remain in the fixed determination to continue the connection between the two countries, not for any selfish British interest, not to gratify Imperial pride, but to secure the happiness and the tranquillity of a united people." Would that our Irish brethren would accept the accomplished facts, of the indissoluble union of these kingdoms, and the rapidly proceeding fusion of races within our frontiers, and, relinquishing the pursuit of the impos- sible, would unite cordially with their English neigh- bours in expediting the advance of all unaccomplished remedial changes that lie within the range of the Constitution

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

I understand that Mr. E. Billingsley, the respected organ- ist of the Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, has compiled, and has now in the press, "a music- ally illustrated service," or what is ordinarily described as "a sacred service of song," entitled "The Basket of Flowers," or "The Triumph of Truth over Falsehood." This gentleman has been very successful in the past in rendering services of songs, and no doubt from his long ex- perience the work will be a good one. The service is to be rendered for the first time in Runcorn.

At the Widnes Police Court on Wednesday a special sessions was held for the purpose of hearing an application fot a theatrical license from a gentleman, who is the manager and proprietor of the "Gaiety" at Winsford. Unfor- tunately, owing to the illness of the applicant,', the matter could not be gone into by the large number of Her Majesty's justices of the peace who were present. Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, senr., expressed some surprise that no gentleman was in attendance to represent the Local Board, as it was proposed to place the building on the Market-place land, which belongs to the local authority. As it was agreed to adjourn the consideration of the application for a week, perhaps Mr. Allen, the clerk to that body, will consider it well to be present on the next occasion. The magistrates expressed a willingness to grant the license if Superinten- dent Barker were satisfied that the building would be prbperly conducted. The love of histrionic matters is, without doubt, very strong in human nature, and if a certain portion of the masses in Widnes cannot be provided with a good theatre, they will go to the bad ones which at times visit the town, where one may occasionally hear such atrocious renderings of plays as the one of which I read the other day where the passage Instead of mounting barbed steeds To fright the souls of fgarful adversaries was rendered, Instead of mounting bare bedsteads, To fright the souls of fearful adversaries Or, by way of variety, I may give another example from the same work—
May yon blew Evin a Poor a down rew-ing a Hon the taratorVed.

Let me hope that such intelligent and literary gentlemen as are to be found upon our local Bench will see to it that the Widnes " Gaiety " is a respectable affair, so that the souls of my friends Mr. Benjamin Brown and Mr. Panirburst may not be roused to a pitch of indignation before which Dr. O'Keeffe will grow dumb, and Mr. Eustace Carey hide his diminished head !

Mr. Thomas Hardie, schoolmaster to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, seems to have l.een guilty of a considerable want of courtesy in addressing to Mr. Coke, vicar of Aston Church, a letter such as that which appears in your columns of last week. Though Mr. Rigby may be inclined to con- sider the communication "a topper "—whatever that may man—it seems very evident that Mr. Hardie has over- stepped the bounds of prudence, and shows a gross want of that respect which is due from one gentleman to another. If the schoolmaster has been in the habit of taking the work. house children to church late, the vicar was quite justified in objecting to have the congregation disturbed in their wor- ship, by the entry of a body of youngsters who would be Pretty sure to enter the sacred building in a rather noisy fashion. jr. Hardie in his very uncalled for letter, in which he characterises the conduct of the vicar, as "a gross piece of impudence," makes a prominent use of the word genteel, the meaning of which is generally understood to be "refined, or well bred ;" but surely after the use of such language, the schoolmaster can scarcely claim to be in- cluded in such a class of persons! What onerous duties can Mr. Hardie have to discharge on Sabbath mornings which should prevent his taking the children to church in time? The Guardians, very rightly, recommended the schoolmaster to offer an apology to the reverend gentleman. FLACCUS.

FIRE AT Rnrrecnnr.—On Saturday night, a curtain in the window of Mr. Thomas Dunbabbin's shop, in Church- street, Runcorn, took iire from the gas, but owing to the energetic efforts put forth by several policemen and neigh- bours, not a very serious amount of damage was done. RUNCORN FOUNTAIN CLOSED.—Runcornians have in the past often had reason to boast of the splendid supply of water obtainable at the fountain, opposite the Town Hall, We regret to state that Dr. Mouritz, the medical officer of health, has had his attention drawn to the water, the use of which he has pronotinced highly injurious to public ;health. The fountain has been temporarily closed.

- - RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS.—The first sewing meeting of a series to be held weekly took place on Wednesday afternoon at the Mission Room, Runcorn. Considerable work was done by the ladies who were present, and it is expected that the meetings will prove very profitable. The following ladies were appointed a Committee :—Mesdames R. Abel, W. Stubbs, T. Houghton, W. Herbert, and the Misses Owen. Miss Williams was appointed hon. secretary and treasurer with Mrs. R. Sealey as assistant. The meet- ings will commence at two o'clock and be continued until 9 p.m. A public tea meeting will be held at six o'clock every Wednesday. All material forwarded to the Mission room will be made up by the ladies and all who are willing and able to assist in the work are earnestly requested to do 80.

WIDNES PAIIISH CHIJECIT SCHOOLS. —SALE OF WORE' —A sale of work was held at Widnes Parish Church school on Thursday and was continued yesterday. The object o f the sale is to augment the classroom fund. For some time past it hfs been a source of complaint that the accommoda- tion in the Waterloo-road Schools was insufficient. This is especially the case in the Girls' School, which is often over- crowded. The Government Inspector has on several occasions pointed out the insufficiency of the present accom- modation and recommended that new class-rooms should be built. In the present schools there is accommodation for 185 boys, 112 girls, and 120 infants, but this is quite in- adequate to the wants of the neighbourhood. There is a plot of land adjoining the school, which was originally given with the-intention of a schoolmaster's house being built upon it. This site will, therefore, be added to the playground, while a portion of the existing playground will he used for the proposed extentions. These will comprise a new infants' class-room, and the extension of the •accom- modation for girls, which will be effected by pulling down the existing infants' class-room and enlarging it. This portion of the building will be carried two storeys high, the upper room to be used for afternoon meetings and general punardoecrhtihal e business.superint Thenaenecesaol of, fe awworokrsk committee, bmiteteene, consisting on of Messrs. Lord, Kilcross, and Jones ; a finance committee, of which Mr. James White, Mr. Treacy, jun. , Crawford, and J. B. Imison were the members. The Rev. J. Wright- Williams, the vicar, and Rev. W. H. Duggan, curate, have also taken a prominent part. The ladies' sewing class, under whose care most of the articles of clothing and fancy-work offered for sale have been made, comprised the following ladies—viz., Mrs. James White, Mrs. Mather, and Mrs. Crawford. The sale was opened by the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams. The schoolroom was used for the sale of work, one of the class-rooms being set apart for the refresh- ment stall, and the other devoted to the various entertain- ments which took place during the day. The stalls were presided over by the following ladies—viz., Mesdames James, White, Crawford, Mather, Lord, Treacey, Kilcross, J. B. Imison, Jones, Shone, and Barton, and the Misses Hed- ley, Lea, and Kendrick. During the day a variety of amuse- ments was provided. Songs, pianoforte solos, and the like formed the staple of the programme. Among those who assisted were Mesdames J. W. Davies, R. White, J. White, and 3. Wright-Williams, the Misses Jones (Runcorn), Lord, Purvet, A. Purvet, Syred, and Wareing; and Messrs. Balmer, Crabtree, Crawford, T. Davies, J. W. Davies, J. B. Imison, Large, Lord, Thorpe, W. Treacey, jun., and A. Wareing.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29,18 L
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29,18 L
WESTON HARVEST FESTIVAL. —The annual harvest festival at Weston Church was held on the night of the 21st inst. The building had been profusely decorated.

SAD DEATH OF AN OLD MAN.-Mr. 3.. E. Worsley, deputy coroner, held an inquiry at the Red Lion Inn, Preston Brook, on Thursday, touching the death of Thomas Pickering Sanders, 60 years of age. From the evidence it seemed that deceased lodged with a woman named Adamson at Preston-o'-th'-hill. He was the worse for drink on Friday night, the 21st inst., and left home about 2-30 next morning saying he was going to Newton, but would be back for breakfast. His landlady cautioned him not to get more drink, and he said he would not. He called at the Red Lion Inn, Halton, where he had a glass of whiskey, and remained about five hours, telling the landlord be was cold and not very well. After leaving the Rod Lion he called at a house and asked permission to sit by the fire and warm himself. He was then drunk. Deceased left the house, and about eight o'clock on Tuesday morning last, his body was found lying in a foot road across some fields in Newton, by Mrs. Hewitt, wife of a farmer. Deceased was without his coat, and his hat and a bottle that had contained whiskey were found lying near him. Dr. Carruthers, of Halloo, said the cause of death was congestive apoplexy, and that death would no doubt have been accelerated by the exposure or drink, if deceased had been drinking. A verdict of "Died from congestive apoplexy," was returned.

A WIDNES CUSTOMS PROSECUTION.—John Hutchin- son and Company, chemical manufacturers, Widnes, and Melville Chambers, Lord-street, were summoned at the in- stance of the Customs authorities, at the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Raffles, for having failed to deliver the necessary return of the exportation of 242 tierces of soda ash, shipped on board the vessel Antwerp, six days after the final clearance of that ship. There were other five informations for similar offences subsequently committed.— Mr. Paxton prosecuted, and stated that the commissioners last year had fined the firm 13 times, and 16 times this year and were compelled to bring these cases now into court.— Mr. James Young, a member of the firm, appeared and pleaded guilty to the charges. He pleaded in extenuation that there was frequent delay in getting the names of the proper vessel by which the goods had been sent. He was not aware, that the firm had been preyiously fined by the commissioners.—Mr. Raffles said that he had come to the conclusion that he had only power to mitigate the fine of £5 in the first offence. He therefore imposed a fine of ss. and costs for the first offence, and £5 and costs for each of the other offences, the total fine amounting to £37 2s.

ENTERTAINMENT BY VIE FARNWORTH AMA.TEUR MINSTRELS.—On Monday evening, the Farnworth Amateur Minstrels gave an entertainment in the Boys' schoolroom. Farnworth. It was the first of the season, but a series of similar entertainments have been given during previous winters and always proved an unqualified success. The proceeds are devoted to charitable purposes. The entertain- ment was opened by a song from Mr. F. C. Davies, which elicited rounds of applause from the audience. It was fol- lowed by "Under the elm tree," which Mr. Whitfield gave with taste and spirit. Mr. T. Foreman gave "The awkward squad," a comic song which caused much amusement. Mr. A. S. Davies' "Agricultural show" was equally well re- ceived ; and a song was also given by Mr. W. Brown. Mr. T. Davies gave "Darling Minnie Lee," and Mr. F. C. Davies " Chillingowallabadore," which he rendered in such a manner as to win a well-deserved encore. A recitation, "Shampoozle," was next given by Messrs. F. C. and A. G. Davies, and heartily applauded. Mr. T. Davies diversified the proceedings by a stump speech. The entertainment, which thi-oughout was most successful, was brought to a close by a farce, entitled "Call at three and I'll make you comfortable," in which Messrs. A. G. Davies, F. C. Davies (who took the two female characters), T. Foreman, S. Smith, C. D. Hunter, and A. Balmer took part. It was well rendered throughout, and the performers sustained the several parts in a manner highly creditable to their memo- ries and taste. Mr. J. Hunter was the conductor during the musical portion of the entertainment: and Mrs. Hunt the accompanist. There was a good attendance.

PENKETH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. —At a meeting of the above class, held on Wednesday last at the Penketh Workmen's Club, Mr. Hobson read a paper on "The liberty of the press." Mr. Albert White presided. Mr. Hobson said in his opening remarks that liberty of speech was the birthright of all true born Britons, and, quoting "Euripides," said— This is true liberty, when free born men Having to advise the public, may speak out, Which he who can and will deserves high praise, Who neither can nor will may hold his peace, What can be juster in a state than this After giving his views on what he believed to be true liberty, he said that without freedom of thought there could be no such thing as wisdom, and without freedom of speech no such thing as public liberty. Freedom of speech was the right of every man as far as by it he did not hurt or control the right of another, and this was the only check which it ought to suffer and the only bounds it ought to know. Freedom of speech produced excellent writers and en- couraged men of genius. The liberty of the press was attended with so few inconveniences that it may be claimed as the common right of all, and that we as a people need not dread any ill consequences from such liberty. No good government who had allowed this freedom of the press had suffered by it, but it wonderfully endeared them to their people. The paper was listened to with great pleasure, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hobson. The following members took part in the debate : Mr. W. 11. Hughes (secretary), Mr. John Manley, &c. The meeting terminated with the usual vote of thanks to the chairman.

The Bishop of Chester presided, on Wednesday, at a conference of the clergy and laiti of his diocese, the first meeting of the kind that has been held since the formation of the see of Liverpool. Bishop Jacobson, referring to this fact, trusted that the division of the diocese would not entail anything like dislocation in their diocesan charities. A favourable report was made by Dean Howson of the working of St. A idan's College, Birkenhead. AUFub DEATII A.T WARRINGTON.—Mr. Driffiold, the county coroner, held an inquest at the Parade Room of the Police Court, on Tuesday morning, to inquire into the cause of death of Nancy Hindley, a widow, 60 years of age, house- keeper for John Wild, labourer, living at 18, Brick-street. About eight o'clock on Sunday morning the deceased was found at the bottom of the stairs, dead. A woman named Sarah Bate, residing in the house adjoining, heard a noise as of a person falling on Saturday night, about ten o'clock. She entered Wild's house, and at the bottom of the stairs she found the deceased, who was groaning. She was "in drink," and Wild and Mrs. Bate endeNvoured to get her to bed. Her answer was, " Let me rest a little while." They stayed with her until twelve o'clock, when Wild went to bed. He had, he stated, left her many times previously in the same condition. She bad never been properly sober for some years. After some deliberation the jury returned a verdict of "Died from suffocation whilst in a drunken state." THE Arzcs.r..x Wears Eno:imams Acv.—The Secre- tary of the Poor Law Board on Tuesday addressed a circular letter to the local sanitary authorities throughout the king- dom inviting their attention to the provisions of the Alkali, Sic., Works Regulation Act, passed last session, and asking to be supplied by the 14th November with full particulars of the various works within their respective jurisdictions, the names and addresses of the proprietors, Bic. It is pointed out that the Act affects not only alkali works but sulphuric acid works, chemical manufacture works, nitrate acid works, sulphate of ammonia works, muriatic ammonia works, and chlorine works, or works in which chlorine, bleaching powder, or bleaching liquor is made, and that after April next works of this character cannot bo carried on unless duly registered. The Act, it is remarked, further provides for the inspection of salt works, in which the extraction of salt from brine is carried on, and to cement works or works in which aluminous deposits are treated for the purpose of making cement. In these cases, however, the Act itself does not impose any limit in regard to the escape of the noxious gases evolved, bat enables the Local Government Board under certain restrictions to require by provisional order that the best means for rendering such gases harmless or in- offensive shall be adopted. VALEDICTORY SERMON OF T Alt REC. RICHARD GREENALL.—The Rev. Richard Greenall, vicar of St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, preach his valedictory I sermon on Sunday evening last to a large congregation. The rev, gentleman preached from the words "And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ "(2 Thessalonians, 3-5), and concluded as follows :—I have been with you nearly six years. It has I been long enough to cement a strong bond of union between us. During that time you have had many trials, in which I hope I have always endeavoured to take part ; and if I have failed in showing sympathy to you under them I pray God to forgive me, and I ask your forgiveness. And I, too, during that time have known something of bitter trials in this place ; but I thank God, I have bad true sympathisers with me. I hope for the sake of those who are to follow me —and I would urge this upon you—ever to sympathize with your clergyman. You little know )vhat he has to go through—the troubles arising not only from his own family but also from the affairs of his parishioners. I tell you that these things during the past six Years I have been with you have made a change in me. They have made i change in my feelings, as also in my health. I look now from another standpoint of view upon the surroundings of this parish as well as of others. But I thank God I am not changed in my affection tovards you, nor for my desire for your welfare both in time and eternity. I shall think of you wherever I may be. For myself I should have keen content to have remained among you, but it happens that I and have others to consult. Ido not think I sahmounlodt lodaornieglt to expect those near and dear to me to con- sent to make such a sacrifice as I might feel bound to make. And remembering that He who knew what was in man has said that a prophet is not without honour save in his own country and in his father's house, I have hopes that there may be better days in store, and that this church may be more amply supported than it has hitherto been. My liiethren, I have now done. I neither wish to work upon my own feelings nor yours. I desire to take an affectionate farewell of you ; and I will close what I have to say from this pulpit with the prayer of the Apostle St. Paul, May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and lute the patient waiting for Christ."
This terminated the business.
RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
ANNUAL SOIREE.

The annual soiree in connection with the Runcorn Parlia- mentary Debating Society was held on Wednesday evening, at the Public Hall. The first part of the proceedings took Place in the ante-room, which, as no fires had been lighted in it, proved cold and most uncomfortable even to most of the male portion of the audience, which, we regret to say, was very meagre. The committee must feel somewhat dis- couraged at the manner in which their efforts to please appear to be appreciated by the general body of the inhabi- tants. Mr. Thomas Handley, the Speaker of the House, presided. The CHAIRMAN said that when the committee met a few weeks ago, it was considered advisable that the session should be opened by a soiree, but, owing to a variety of cir- cumstances, it could not be held on the date fixed, and had to be adjourned for two or three weeks. It often happened that when a gatherine, was adjourned, it did not go with the same Terve as it wouid have done if held at the time origi- nally appointed and this appeared to be the case with their meeting that night. He wished to urge the young men present to take a greater interest in the Debating Society than they had done heretofore. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He might make this appeal on educational and also on patriotic grounds. (Hear.) All Englishmen ought to take an interest in the welfare of their country ; and one of the first duties of members of a Parliamentary Debating Society was to make themselves acquainted with the history of their countty. He was not too old to feel a pleasure in many of the pastimes which occupied young men. (Hear, hear.) He might observe that games of chance should not be the only occupation of leisure hours. (Hear, hear.) If young men took an interest in such societies as that, it would enlarge their minds, cause them to take an interest in passing events, and lead them to form opinions on one side or the other in politics which they considered would prove of benefit to the country which they all loved. (Applause.) During the evening, the PRIME MINISTER (Mr. William Handley) delivered a few interesting remarks. He said the main purpose of their meeting that night was, next to having a re-union of the Members, to enlist the sympathies of the audience on behalf of the society. He should like to see a larger attendance in future than there had been during the present session, and with such an accession of strength they would be enabled to carry on the work of the session with a fair prospect of success. He wished to plead for a larger number of members on the Conservative side of the House, and surely it would be a very easy thing to obtain them after the great accession of strength which it was stated had come ,1 to the party through the recent revision in Runcorn. (A ' laugh, and hear, hear). The Liberals would be glad if the ,1 members of the ornosite party would come forward mid °lye tiieili tide beneflt of their vivice in matters In which tiley I were understood to be to lamentably deficient. (Laughter). It was well known that many of the public men who were leaders of the people, had first tried their wings in the local arena of debating societies. It was in such associations that they Qrst learned to form opinions upon public matters, and this early training had resulted in their becoming a power in the world. If they joined the society and worked in con- nection with it they would have the satisfaction of feeling that they had donwomething to help the young men of the day to form sound pinions on current questions, and this contributed to advance the social and political life of the country. (Applause). When a man's words dropped from his lips, they were something like the pebble thrown into the lake, which continued to make its circles until they reached the boundary of the water. So it was impossible to tell what might be the effect of such an association in help- ing forward thepolitical education of the men of the future. (Applause). Mr. SHORE, the Leader of the Opposition, afterwards uttered 7a few telling remarks, spiced with considerable humour. He was glad to say that during previous sessions the members of the two partiec bad not destroyed themselves, like the two Kilkenny cats. In fact, he believed it was part of the unwritten code that on such occasions they should be like the Romans spoken of in Horatius, when none were for a party, but all were for the State. He would remind his somewhat facetious friend, Mr. Handley, that the members of the Conservative party had on several occasions proved too many for their opponents. (Hear, hear, and applause). Runcorn had led the van in that district in the formation of a Pailiamentary Debating Society, and he considered that it would not reflect upon either party, or upon the town, if, after a certain number of years, the society were not to be continued, because the amount of natural efflux from such an organisation necessarily required a very large population to find a number of gentlemen who had the time to take part in it. In conclusion, he expressed a hope that they would have a very satisfactory session. (Applause). Mr. F. A. LAKE also made a few remarks. During the evening Mrs. Shore, Miss James, and Mr. K. Morris sang various songs, to the accompaniment of Miss Jukes and Mr. Ravenscroft. Mr. James Craig, BA.' master of the Collegiate school, gave a reading in a very finished and humourous style. Mr. W. Cameron, of Overton, caused much amusement by singing several comic songs. Messrs. W. Kay and W. R. Karp also gave a selection upon the . .
Thereat of the evening was spent in dancing in the large hall. Mr. Lightbarn, jun., acted a MC., and Mr. Ravens- croft presided at the piano.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. There were present :—Mr. T. Sutton-Timmis (in the chair), the Revs. G. Holloway, T. Finegan, James Clarke, Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, Hartland, Shaw, and Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

Mr. DEACON read the report of this committee, from which it appeared that during September 326 parents had been summoned before the committee, of which 107 were applications for payment of fees, and 219 for contravention of the Education act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 80 cases. Three of the applications were adjourned for further enquiries, and 24 refused. Mr. HARTLAND sug- gested that a plan ought to be adopted by which those parents who were in the habit of frequently coming before the committee, could be dealt with by attendance officers, as their repeated applications and ridiculous excuses. entailed , a great deal of unnecessary and fruitless labour.—Mr. DEA- CON argued that the plan proposed by Mr. Hartland could not be carried out, as the magistrates would not convict in cases where it was not clearly proved that the person prose- cuted had been before the committee several times.—Mr. SHAW believed that this course of action on the part of the Bench simply arose from the system of red tape into which all such official proceedings seemed to run.—The discussion then dropped.

PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT RUNCORN.

A sum of nearly £5O being due to the treasurer of the Runcorn Greenway-road Chapel, the friends belonging to that place of worship determined upon making an effort, or a series of efforts, to raise the suM. Consequently a society meeting was called, when a committee was appointed with power to design and carry out whatever scheme they might deem best to secure the end in view. They very wisely decided in the first instance to bring the ladies' element in the congregation into full prominence by appealing to those who position in life would allow them to give 'trays" at a public tea meeting to do so. This appeal was met with a ready response. A somewhat new feature was brought out to excite a keenness in the competition for the sale of tickets. Each of the ladies referred to was given 18 tickets, which was the number her table would seat. Each ticket had upon it the number of a particular table, so that each person to whom she sold a tick& would come to her table. In any case, it was provided that each lady must give up 18s. as the result of her table. The " oracle " worked well, as all the tickets were disposed of before the day fixed upon. The tea meeting took place in the Regent-street Schoolroom on Wednesday afternoon, when the building was decorated with flags, which gave it a pleasant appearance. The tables were very tastefully laid out, and the good things had been provided with an unsparing hand, which reflected the greatest credit on all concerned. Fully 250 sat down to tea. The following ladies gave trays and pre- sided at the tables :—Mrs. J. Pickwell, Mrs. E. Billingsley, Mrs. T. Booth, Mrs. R. Collier' Mrs. S. White, Mrs. Jas. Stubbs, Mrs. Fleet, Miss A. Moores, Mrs. Ruscoe, Mrs. Broadhurst, and Mrs. E. Faulkner. An extra table was pro- vided for late corners, which was presided over by Mrs. Lewis. After tea, a public meeting was held, which was very largely attended. The Rev. J. Pickwell, introduced the Chairman, Councillor Allman, of Crewe (who is a Primitive Methodist), to the meeting. This gentleman gave a good speech which was received with great heartiness.—The CHAIRMAN next called upon Mr. E. Billingsley, who had acted as secretary to the committee, to read the result of their efforts.—Mr. BILLINGSLEY said it was a great pleasure to give the result of the efforts put forth, and which had brought about so encouraging a result. Never had he been so heartily received as during his late canvass, and he hoped the dawn of a prosperous time had commenced with them. The ladies had done their part grandly and had made that meeting the most successful one they had ever had. He then gave the amount realised at each table, and also read the list of donations so far given, which was as fol- lows:—Total amount received from ladies for their tables, £ll 173.; donations received £6 55.; making a total of £lB 2s. (Loud applause.) He bad thought if they raised £l5 they would do well, but, on second thoughts, he should not be satisfied unless they raised £2O. He believed that this sum would be easily realised during the week. (Loud applause.)—The CHAIRMAN next called upon Mr. H. Hinde, of Norley, and Mr. Jos. Spruce, of Preston Brook; the Rev. D. Schofield, and the Rev. Joseph Pickwell (the two latter being the circuit ministers), to address the meeting; and their remarks were very well received.—The :choir gave selections of sacred music during the evening.—Mr. Bil- lingsley, the chapel organist, presided it the harmonium with his customary taste and ability.—The usual votes of thanks were passed, which brought a most successful meet- ing to a close. We understand the next effort to reduce the debt will be special sermons, which will be preached early in December, and be followed by a service of song, compiled by Mr. E. Billingsley, which we look forward to with pleasure. The three efforts are expected to yield the required amount. We wish our. Primitive Methodist friends at Runcorn every success.

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT PRESCOT.—The distribution of prizes to the successful competitors in the annual firing competition of R Company (late 48th of the 21st (St. Helens) L.R.V., held in September last took place on Thursday, in the Assembly- rooms, Prescot. There was on parane one officer, six sergeants, and twenty-five rank ani file, together with fourteen band and buglers; total, forty-six. There were in all twenty-nine prizes, ranging in amount from 2s. 6d. to 20s. The captain's alive? challenge cup was car- ried off for the second time by Corporal John Jackson, whose property it now becomes, and the large brass pan, presented by Mr. T. Prescott, ironmonger, of the Market- place, was won by Sergeant Roughsedge. Captain Cross announced his intention of presenting another cup for com- petition next season. The prizes were distributed by Mrs. Cross.
