Poort RATES—The following poor rates were sanctioncd,l on the application of the assistant overseers :—Aston-bv- Sutton Bd. in the £, Aston Grange lid., and Stockliam 0. in the £. A Fxsit DEALER OBSTRTCTING THE STREET.—TIIOIII:I9 Smith, fish dealer, was summoned for causing an obstruction in Church-street with his donkey and cart. P.C. Noden said that on the night of the 15th inst., he was in Church- street, at about eleven o'clock, when he saw the defendant's donkey and cart obstructing the footpath, so that people had to go round them in order to pass. He spoke to defen- dant, but when he attempted to go on, the donkey fell upon its knees twice. He asked Smith what was amiss with it, on which be replied that it was badly troubled with rheumatic in its legs.—ln reply to Superintendent William- son, the officer said that he had been instructed to take par- ticular notice of the defendtrit in consequence of numerous complaints having been made about the street being obstructed. Defendant let his donkey and cart remain at the spot from five minutes to eleven to a quarter past.—De- fendant said the prosecution was merely a matter of spite against him. He paid £4 a year to Government for a hawk- ing licence, and he thought it very hard that be should be summoned for staying a few minutes to deliver something at a public house and get a glass of beer.—The Chairman said it would not take defendant twenty minutes to get a glass of beer and deliver an article at the publichouse. t He had been fined in the past for a similar offence, but the amount he had had to pay did not appear to have had any deterrent effect upon him. He would now be fined 10s. and costs Hs. 6d., or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment. The money was paid. A FAMILY Dis-ronnexcx.—A young man named Peter Carter, who appeared with a black eye, was summoned for threatening to assault James Chambers, on the 20th inst. Complainant said he was the defendant's father-in-law, and about a quarter past ten on the night mentioned, he went to bed. At twenty minutes after eleven o'clock, he was awoke by hearing a noise in the house. He went down stairs' and found the defendant there, with a pint of beer before him. He said to him "Peter, you don't live here," and he replied "Yes I do; I am a lodger." He told defendant he was not going to allow him to make such rows in his house, and that he must leave. Defendant then said that if he did not go outside he would knock his neck out. He replied that he should fetch a policeman to eject him. Defendant answered that he did not care if he brought forty policemen. He then sent for one, who put defendant out of the house. The young man was idle, dissolute, and in the habit of working about four months in the summer, and then making his home with his mother during the winter. He and his brother made a custom of visiting the house, when he (de- fendant) was out, and getting food which they had not earned.—Elizabeth Lawrenson said she had been employed for some weeks at the dwelling next to complainant's and on the night referred to she heard him assaulting his wife, who begged him not to strike her upon the face. From her ex- perience of complainant, she was of opinion that he was very quarrelsome and treated his wife and children badly. She did not, however, appear to be in a position to give any evidence as to what took place on the particular night in question.—Joseph Carter, brother of defendant, gave evidence in his favour.—The Chairman said Carter had been bound over once for common assault, another time for threatening, and had also been fined for drunkenness. If be had any grievance against his father-in-law, it would be a far wiser course for him to find some other home, as he professed to be able to keep himself. He would now be bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties in £5, and have to pay 13s. 6d. costs, or, in default, be committed one month to prison. A SHOEMARER CHARGED WITH FELONY.—James Clarke, a respectably dressed man employed at the American Boot and Shoe Manuisctory, Ellesmere-street, was brought up charged with steeling a coat, value 55., the property of Patrick Whelan; and a .pair of shoes belonging to Mr. Francis Clarke, who trades under the rather high soundine, name given above. Whelan said that on Sunday night the prisoner, who had been in the habit of visiting the house , regularly to have cooking done for him, came there about seven o'clock, and put on the coat, after which he asked the daughter if she did not think he looked well in it. Prisoner went out wearing the garment, and he (witness) walked to to the police office about the matter.—P.C. Bossons gave evidence to the effect that he apprehended the prisoner on Sunday evening, on the platform of the L. and N. W. station at Widnes. He was wearing the coat, had the boots under his arm, and had booked to Liverpool.—Joseph Smazeo manager to the American Boot Co., gave evidence which did not throw much light upon the case. He, however, was inclined to think that the prisoner's story that he had met a woman near Waterloo bridge, upon goiag home on SatirdaY night, who gave him the boots to return to the shoe, was correct; and that he would have returned to work ds Mon- day morning.—The evidence of the prosecutor Whelan, who appeared in court in a most tatterdemalion dress, caused some amusement, the general opinion apparently being that it was somewhat strange that an individual attired in such a worn out garb, had a coat worth stealing.—Mr.Brundrit said there was a good deal of suspicion attaching to the prisoner

lin both cases, but as, in the opinion of the Bench, there was not sufficient evidence to show a felonious intent, he would be set at liberty. ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO EVADE RENT.—WilliaM Dono- van, who did not put in an appearance, was summoned for clandestinely removing his goods from a house belonging to Mr. Charles Dutton, Market Inspector. The complainant asked the magistrates to adjourn the case a month, as de- enda nt had agreed to come to an arrangement.

div.head: WARRINGTON fARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON fARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

The society held a meeting on Monday evening, the speaker (Dr.Huson-More) in the chair. The benches on the Ministe- rial side of the House were well filled, but the Opposition was represented by some dozen members.—The Premier, on behalf of the membet for Newcastle, gave notice that ke would ask the Home Secretary "if he can name the day fE r the introduction of the proposed Licensing Bill of the Go- vernment ; and if it is in his province to give any forecast of the nature thereof."—Tbe right bon. member for Truro then rose to move "That this house is of opinion that the application of the principles which govern our commercial system ought to be reconsidered with a view to re-adjustment in order to prevail upon foreign countries to reduce their tariffs on the products of industry exported from this coun- try." He said he took it for granted that hostile tariffs were injurious to the trade of the country, and it was con- ceded on all sides that the existence of commercial treaties was the cession of that principle, because their only object was to get their tariffs as low as possible. It had been said that if America adopted Free Trade, and the hostile tariffs were removed, it would be the beginning of the time when the commercial prosperity of England would be transferred to the other side of the Atlantic. Ile had no fear of such a consummation. (Hear, bear.) He did not believe that protective tariffs were any security for our commercial pros- perity, and their reduction was desirable. He went on to show that commercial treaties were a system of retaliation, and said he wanted to see a fair, wise, and statesmanlike ap- plication of the principles for which he ntended. He did not think it was just to exclude any class from the benefits which might be derived from a re- adjustment of our commercial system-(hear, hear)-and yet a member opposite would pass his veto upon it if there was any fear that sixpence of the five shillings the working- man might obtain, going into the landlords' pockets. The inducement to abolish the Corn Law was that other nations would follow our example, and take our manufactures duty free. He need not say that that prediction had been falsi- fied. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Cobden's policy had so far'been a fellacy. (No, no.) He did not deny that benefits had dccrued from the policy of 1846, but we had at that time everything to gain and nothing to lose. But times were changed, and foreign countries were to a great extent inde- pendent Of our manufactures, and we had rivals in foreign markets. Other countries had become more protective, and the same progress had been made in those countrire as in England. (No, no.) In his opinion the present policy had not been a success, and Dlr. Ecroyd's scheme—(oh, oh)—of forming a Free Trade Conferation with our colonies was one which deserved fair consideration. A small fixed duty on corn might increase the price of the loaf slightly; it would be a certain- amount out of a man's wages, but he already paid a certain amount for tea. It was a question of great importance, and he did not think it should be shelved. It was a working man's question for the simple reason that our capitalists could invest their money abroad and the working man could not.—The member for North-East Lancashire , seconded the motion.—The President of the Board of Trade said the resolution was the old monster protection, which was aiming at the reversal of our cominer- cial policy, roaring at our commercial pree- parity and seeking to destroy our commeiclal supremacy. Eight years ago the leaders of the party opposite were exclaiming for Free Trade and all its attendant blessings; now there was nothing too hard to say aeainst it, and the temporary check to our commercial relations was attributed to its cause. There was an excess of imports over exports in England of 125 millions, and it was argued that there was a continual drain of gold from the country. It was, however, accounted for by the ability of our merchants to invest their capital abroad, and the interest from that investment was no less than 45,000,000 annually. There was also the profits and our carrying trade, which brought it up to 117,000,000. He pointed out that the tariff on French wines was merely for revenue purposes, and showed that while the exports had been fall- ing off until 18W, they were now on the increase, and entirely confuted the statement that the trade was going out of the country. (Applause.) The same thing existed with regard to the home trade. It was difficult to decide what remedies they should adopt with regard to commercial rela- tions. Manufacturers advocated a tax upon minufactured goods; the agricelturist upon food ; whilst the Leader In the House of Commons advocated a tax all round. The total imp, Is represented 01 per cmt. of food and raw materials, land hard 9 p2e cent, of manufactured goods; and our if experts cons'qt.?(l of 92 per cent, of manufactured articles, I and 8 per cent, of raw materialS. Therefore they would inflict no great injury by taxing our manufactured produce, but by taxing our food they would inflict gross injury on the nation at large. (Applause.)—The Chief Secretary for India compared the member for Truro to Sir Stafford Northcote in having failed to declare what he meant. Ho asked that the Fair Trade policy might take a definite shape, so that they might understand its objects. There was not a member on his side the bouse who had read the history of Free Trade, and knew the life of Richard Cobden, but was prepared to push their principles as far as they could, and where they were stopped by protective powers, to do their best with them. (Hear, hear.) The speech of Sir Stafford Nortlicote at Newcastle could he summed up in these word., "My dear people, defend us poor landlords." (Laughter.) In his opinion the question of Fair Trade had been promulgated by landlords to draw the people's attention from the real subject—the land ques- tion. (Applause.) They wanted a peasant proprietary, but they never would have one if the Conservatives had their way. (Applause.) No protective duty was placed upon imports from China; we did not grow tea, and protected DO home trade in that direction. Referring to the Bradford trade, he said it could not be proved that Free Trade had injured its trade, and concluded bee saying that he was satis- fied the people would re ect the Fair Trade notion. (Applause.)—The member for Montrose, in as energetic and fo"cible speech, said he disclaimed to look upon it from a party point of view. He was a Free Trader. rho question presented itself in two aspects, the aspect of the political economist, and of the statesman. After giving a definition of Free Trade and Reciprocity, the ;meeker said retaliation was an act oh war—(hear, hear,)—and from an economic point of view was wrong. Then might the question be asked, "Does the position of the commerce of this country justify us by proceeding upon an act of war?" He said it did not. (Hear, hear.) Referring tethe remarks of the member for Truro, he said when he proved to him that America, France, and Germany had increased in material wealth more than this country, then he would begin to believe in Reciprocity. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Until then he should remain a Free Trader. But be would prove that the reverse was the fact; that Germany and France, with their competition in our own markets, had suffered from commer- cial depression with ourselves. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had suffered from the inflation of prices in 1874 and 1875, and the extension of credit thereon. In the years 18734-5, he knew from persanal experience that emigrants returned from America in tAftft ooahhmrceo surraumor America anvnne ergds iwhstedhaoa; that ttebpr protection thatagain,cotr t districts protective. wehte, iasaviskatoeinla.ladl,ne skilled hanateseihrsweh the farmer had the means to sell and the means to buy. Yet he was sorry to say. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He tried with us in this country, had sent farm implements of all descriptions, but had she sent them at a profit ? He denied most emphatically that they had been sold at a profit. Pig iron was 50 to 80 per cent, per ton higher in America than in England, and wages were from 50 to 100 per cent. higher, and they could not compete with us in the markets of the world. But they did compete. And who paid the piper ? The poor people at home. It was not long ago since he went to Germany to negotiate a contract with a firm, but before the directors could move one foot they had to go to Berlin to consult with the bank. Every brick of the place was mortgaged, and they could not negotiate a contract of the extent he wished without having to go 300 miles to ask to do it. At that time manufacturers in Germany went down like ninepins. He denied that France had increased. Adverting to shipping trade, he said prior to the civil war America carried 75 per cent of the produce that we imported and exported; now she carried nothing, and was entirely in the hands of this country. In 1869 we carried 52 per cent. of the world's commerce, to-day we carried 55 per cent.— an amount greater than Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, Scandinavia, Spain, and the United States, and we should occupy the position so long as we adhered to Free Trade principles. (Loud cheers,) The reason was because the materials from which ship were built cost in America Ifrom 50 to 65 per cent. more than they cost in England, —(hear, hear)—and 40 long as we could has e our materials supplied at the cheapest rate, we should always be able, in spite of that bugbear competition, to hold our own in the markets of the world. Once begin to tax food, and the cost of productien was enhanced. (Applause.) Goods paid for goods, and they must not let £ 8. d. come into account at all ; if they did, they were bound to get wrong. The trade of the world was one gigantic tarter, and if we interfered with our relations in any way—by enhancing the cost of living or of articles preduced, our commercial supremacy woeld begin to decline. (Loud applause.)—The house then resolved itself into committee.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A Central News Paris telegram of Friday says it has been virtually decided by the leaders of the Land League move- ment to make Paris the leading quarters of the organisation and to carry on the work from here. A number of Irish M.P.'s and others connected are now in the capital, and it has been decided at a conference just held to continue the agitation fearless of whatever action the Government may take.

At a meeting of the Sliding Scale Committee of South Wales and Monmouthshire, at Cardiff, yesterday, it waS resolved to grant 21- per cent, wages advance to all colliers in the association from November Ist.

The International Fishery Conference, which has been sitting at the Hague during the last three wteks, held its concluding meeting yesterday. An agreement has been arrived at for theestablishment of efficient police regulations in the North Sea, which, if adopted by the various govern- ments of England, France, Germany, Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, are expected to be sufficient to regulate the disorders which have of late been unfortun- ately too frequent among fishermen in the North Sea. The suggestions of Her Majesty's Government have been in the main adopted, and British delegates leave Holland next week.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SCARLET FEVER AT WARRINGTON.

The British Medical Journal of October 22nd, 1881, says —A considerable epidemic of scarlet fever is now raging at Warrington, where, thanks to the Local Act of 1879, pro- viding for the compulsory notification of cases of infectious disease, the dimensions of the outbreak can be pretty accurately gauged. The number of cases in the borough which was 12 in the month of June, rose to 15 in July, to 36,in August, and 62 in September. The Sanitary Commit. tee are making strenuous efforts to limit the extension of the disease by isolation of the patients, under the special clause of the local Act, which enables the authority to dispense with the necessity of a justice's order for compulsory removal, except in cases where definite refusal to consent to such removal has been made; and which also provides that any case may be compulsorily removed where the sufferer is "without proper lodging or accommodation, enabling the case to be properly isolated so as to prevent the spread of the disease and to be properly treated." This, as Mr. Ernest Hart Las pointed out, in his recent report on Local Legislation as to Infectious Diseases (volume i' 1881, p. 380, sets at rest a point which the General Public Health Act leaves ambiguous, since the clause now pursuance e dangero f his 'applies without question to all cases where the patients ntoanoihnnetrbs.nnl thh,omineps duty in securing the isolation of cases of this description, Thepro) seems to have incurred the displeasure of a certain section of the Town Council, who tools the opportunity of the Sani- emrleyafteraelatoedffiactetrhoefirHoena- tary Committee's expenditure of a sum of money for two hospital tents (in supplement of the resources of the perma- nent hospital) being brought up for confirmation, to endea- vour to pass a resolution virtually condemnatory of their action. Fortunately these efforts were not successful ; but it says little for the wisdom of some of the town councillors that, with an epidemic of scarlatina impending over them, they should raise an unseemly wrangle as to the propriety of what cannot but be considered as a most judicious and bene- ficial expenditure by the Sanitary Committee, There can be little doubt that, by the isolation which could his effected by the use of these tents, the town has been saved a vastly larger cost in the shape of suffering, misery, and death, which the unchecked presence of scarlet fever in its midst must inevitably have entailed.

div.head: PUDDLERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: PUDDLERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.

- - - The puddlers employed at the Bewsay Forge, of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., have struck work in consequence of a dispute as to the scale of wages. From what we have been able to gather, it appears that fora long time the men have been working what is known as "part cinder," for which they were paid Bs. ton, and they state that the employers wished to change the quality of the iron, and introduce what is called "all mine fettling." By this change a reduction of 3d. a ton would be effected in the wages of the men, who allege that after a fortnight's trial, it has proved detrimental to them. Besides the reduction in price the puddlers complain that the new material is of lighter weight and demands more labour than the quality they have hitherto had, and that this is equivalent to a double rednction in the rate of wages. The men say that having suffered reduction after reduction, they consider that in the face of a rising market the action of the employers in trying to effect another reduction was most unjustifiable. They, therefore, decline to accept the new terms, and left work. In the course they have taken the puddlers state they have the sympathy of the men in Lancashire at large, and what is most important, promises of support. On the part of the employers it is asserted that it is the cus- tom in the iron trade to pay a certain scale of prices for puddling, and a certain addition in respect to the sort of "fettling" used. The present price of puddling is 7s. 3d. per ton, and for what is termed "cinder fettling" 6d. per ton extra is paid; for part "mine" and part "cinder" 3d. per ton; but where " all mine" is used no extra is paid. This, they say, is the recognised custom of the trade, and has always been followed in Warrington. Some of the pud- dlers at Bewsey Forge have been working part " mine " and part " cinder" at the regular extra of 3d. per ton. A change is now proposed by the employers, who desire to work all "mine fettling" at the trade price without the extra. The men object to work under this arrangement, although we are given to understand that it is a well-established custom and makes no change Whatever in the scale of wages, and that other men are now at work on the same terms both at the Dallam Forge of the same company and under other em- ployers in the town. By this unfortunate dispute some 50 shinglers and others, besides the 180 puddlers and "under hands," are thrown idle, but we are glad to learn that there is no likelihood of the mills stopping. Both parties appear equally resolved not to give way, and a mass meeting of the men will be held to-day.

div.head: SINGULAR PROPERTY DISPUTE AT
div.p: SINGULAR PROPERTY DISPUTE AT

ST. HELENS. In the Lancashire Court of Chancery, Manchester, on Saturday, the Vice-Chancellor gave judgment in the action Morecroft T. Evans, with the hearing of which he had been occupied seven or eight days at the Liverpool sittings. The plaintiff was George Morecroft, a collier, and the defendanti were Messrs. Richard Evans and Sons, colliery proprietors Haydock.—His Honour said the relief sought by the plain- tiff in the action was two-fold, and related to two transac- tions in different years. According to his own story, the plaintiff in January, 1855, enclosed, as an encroachment from certain waste land called Parr Moss, in the township of Parr, in St. Helens, two pieces of land, one containing seven statute acres and the other four Cheshire acres. It was with the former of these pieces of land that the court had to deal. The plaintiff further alleged that in the month of January, 1875, he would have acquired, had he remained unmolested, a good title by adverse possession of the land in question. Mr. Evans, having acquired the rights of lord of the manor, instructed his agent to obtain from the "squatters," including the plaintiff, an secknowledgment of his title, and to call upon the plaintiff. On the 24th March, 1874, the plaintiff executed a deed of that date, which, by the first paragraph of the prayer of his statement of claim, he now sought to have declared fraudulent and void, and delivered up to him. The grounds on which he sought this relief were—(l) That he was grossly deceived by the agents of the defendants, in whom , he had placed .confictence 3nd trust; (2) That the defendants and their agents knew that in nine months from the execution of the deed the plaintiff would be the absolute owner of the property worth, by reason of the minerals beneath the surface of the land, some 0,000 or £B,OOO, and that the defendants or their agents induced him by misrepresentation to execute the deed or "some in- strument" in ignorance of its nature or effect ; and (3), That the:defendant obtained in a grossly improper manner a receipt from the plaintiff's wife, unknown to the plaintiff, and that such receipt was in some way evidence of the defendants' fraud, or at all events, could not be relied upon to support the deed. There were also in the statement of claim certain general charges against the defendants of threat said to have been used by their agents to turn off from their employment the plaintiff and his sons, unless the plaintiff complied with the defendants' wishes by executing the deed.—The Vice- Chancellor reviewed the evidence in the case at considerable length, and in announcing the conclusions be had arrived at said that in his judgment the averments on the plaintiff's part as to threats were not substantiated, and must therefore be disregarded. He was further of opinion that there was no fraud whatever practised on the plaintiff when he executed the deed of March 24, 1874. There was no ground whatever for impeaching the deed, and the plaintiff's case fell entirely upon that head. Then as to the second deed, of May 18, 1877, if the former deed stood it went a long way toward saying that the latter deed must stand also, It had been ' peached on various grounds, none of which in his (the chancellor's) opinion had been substantiated. The the plaintiff, therefore, wholly fell, and rhis ac' be dismissed with costs.

div.head: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.

ET A SOIJTH-WF.ST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SPlcter.] No. =I. • yEzREEL, SHUNEM, AND NAIN TO NAZARETH. We crossed over the plain to Shunem early next morning, and found it a wretched village. Making our way through I its outskirts and over the hill without stopping, we passed round the western spur of the Little Hermon and came to rain. Here we found, in the midst of dirty modern sur- roundings, many indications of an ancient origin. The remnants of massive walls, thickly overgrown with white moss, spoke of a history reaching back into the far past; and beyond the walls of the ruined city, was the appdtrance of an old burial ground to which the funeral procession would be making its way as Christ came in from Caper- mourn. Within the space of one hour we had visited two scenes of bereaved motherhood, in which the children were called back to life amid circumstances of inimitable tender- ness. The least robust of the party lingered at Nain, pondering and conversing on these interesting themes, while the others rode round the centre of the plain and pro- ceeded in the direction of Nazareth. As we came nigh the Lace of the hill on the ridge of which Nazareth sits, we were somewhat appalled by the steepness and ruggedness of the ascent. We had seen nothing like it before in Palestine. We had clambefed about half way up the hill when one of the ladies who rode immediately before me thought she saw an easier path than the one the guide was leading us, and struck off into it. Of coarse my pony followed, and the consequence was that we soon came to a dead stand— the road was so frightfully precipitous both before and behind us. Then we heard loud voices calling upon us not to proceed. They might have saved their breath, for the thing bad become impossible. We dared not even dismount until one of the Arabs came. He then conducted us over fearfully rough rocks and narrow ledges to the top of the I hill. We soon forgot the peril we had escaped as we stood and looked over the magnificent plain we had left behind; but more deeply engrossing were our emotions as we passed down the age-worn paths that lead into the town. We remembered we were now gazing on scenes which had been familiar to the eves of the sinless One—now the Lord of the universe—for thirty years. Here in this beautiful upland vale, with nearly the whole of Palestine under the range of His bodily vision, the Saviour grew in favour with both God and man. Here He, whose rightful place was in the highest heaven, was seen in lowly loving intercourse with men. In childhood's innocency and manhood's grace He bowed—though King of kings and Lord of lords—to take a lowly servant's place—to serve, to suffer, and obey. The town looked very enchanting as we descended the valley, occupying as it does the base and ridge of a precipitous hill behind. Our tents were visible on a green sward to the right of the town, but we had to pass through the outskirts of the town to reach them. In doing so we came to the celebrated well so often mentioned by travelers, and around which were gathered, on this ever-to-be-remembered Satur- day evening, a great number of women, young and old, chattering like so many magpies, whilst those nearest to the spent of the fountain were struggling for priority. Our sudden appearance amongst them created a pause and a good deal of curiosity. Most of the young women were dart-eyed and gipsy-li'm in feature. One of the quieter Madonna-like maidens, in compliance with our request, brought a little vessel filled with water two or three times. Then we passed on, and as we sat resting after the fatigues of the day, and admiring the beauty of the scene, the chimes of the church bells broke upon our ears, and we felt more really at home than we had done since we had left the shores of Old :`:agland.

NAZARETH. On our way to Nazareth we had seen, moving along the ridge of a distant hill to the left, a long and curious string of travellers, mostly on foot, but with ono here and there mounted on a pony or an ass. The streets of Nazareth, the same evening, revealed to us the nature of the procession. Fourteen hundred Russian pilgrims had arrived in the town on that day, so that, instead of finding, the old city a quite secluded spot, we found its narrow, many-cornered, uneven streets crowded with these hardy • sons and daughters of the north. Various groups of them were collected before the open bazaars bargaining with coins in their hands—their only interpreters—for oranges, then cakes, etc., etc. We saw one insolent tradesman casting back their money and snatching the articles oat of their hands. The young men of the town were perambulating the streets in twos and threes, evidently with the purpose of making sport out of the poor strangers, pushing against them in the crowded thoroughfares, with other acts of rudeness. We ascertained from an English resident that the influx of the Russian devotees does not at all tend to good order and morality in the town, but the re- verse, indeed, that the state of society in Nazareth was be- coming worse and worse every year, and that it was trace- able in a great degree to the gross immorality of the pilgrims. The impression they had made upon me, wherever we met them. was that they were a simple-minded people; yet we could not discredit the testimony of one who was daily brought into contact with the poorer classes in Nazareth, and had the most intimate knowledge of all its affairs. The Russian government, by affording many travelling facilities to these pilgrimages, gives great encouragement to the poorer portions of their people to visit Palestine. Whether the object is to create an enthusiasm for the Holy Land, as well as for the holy places in Jerusalem„ so as to prepare them for its occupation in due time, I cannot say; but when a nation goes out of its way to encourage its people in sending money away from home, suspending labour, which is also money, at the same time, on behalf of a sentiment, it is perhaps neither unnatural nor unreasonable to look beyond the fact for a more than sentimental purpose. The native guide who undertook to conduct us through the city was a curiosity. He waajitall and spare, with white hair and eye-lashes. His dress nme composed of a short sac of brown cloth, from which descended a sort of calico petticoat, without folds, reaching to his feet. To a great deal of apparent simplicity, be added a wonderful amount of coolness and audacity. When we visited the church of the Annunciation, he led us right up to the flower-bedecked altar, within a narrow chapel, where the worshippers were kneeling and kissing the ground on which they say Mary received the angel Gabriel. When we paused for fear of intruding he beckoned us forward, and, while the people were prostrate at our feet, he began to ex- plain, without any whispering, the various objects before us. All this the guides think, is in the way of business. They pay the Turkish Government a large sum for their license, and they consider it gives them the right to pursue their calling without any regard to,the feelings of the worshippers, and strange to say, some of them think it imposes the duty of implicit belief in Christian and Mahometan worship, and reliquie alike. The Latln church professes to show you the work-shop of Joseph, and the kitchen of Marv, the former quite a modern structure, and the latter a dark chamber, cut in the rock, which has the appearance of having been an old cistern, whose mouth at the top they declare to be a chimney. Of course no one can deny the antiquity of the rock, nor successfully contend against the date of the ex- cavation, so we had better pass on to the synagogue. And here we stand in silent awe to think that within this plain and simple edifice, very much as it nor appears, the boy of twelve would ask and answer questions, even as he ' did in Jerusalem; the young man, between twenty and thirty, would probably surprise by his wisdom, while he awed by the purity of his life. Here also, on his return from the Jordan, where he had been acknowledged and anointed by the Father, the same Holy Child, the Son of the living God, claimed to fulfil in his own person the glowing predictions of Isaiah with reference to the Messiah, and up these very steps on which we stand, and which lead into the street, the meek and lowly One was hustled and ousted by the excited elders, and dragged hence to the brow of the hill by the infuriated populace. If my readers ask why I am so confident about the synagogue and so doubtful about other places, I answer that the interior of the synagogue strikes you, the moment you enter, as being one of the oldest lauildin,gs you ever saw. And, inasmuch as its history is traceable as far back as A.D. 570, I see no reason why it should not have a pro-Christian origin. A plain, solid structure, preserved as this has been for 1,300 years, would be but little worse in 500 or 600 years more. The synagogue stands in the very centre of the town. A zigzag of three streets forms the market place, and the synagogue is in the centre. On entering the place you descend a flight of about eight steps, which run across the interior. Upon the bottom step rests a row of monolithic pillars, black and pitted with age. The body of the building is capable of accommodating ebout a hundred persons, but the only gets are the low forms that project from the walls and rurt round the room. Seated on these were a few poor-looking men, one of whom was reading quite audibly, and with great rapidity, from a book that lay on his knee. We thought this might boa privilege still granted to the Jews, although the synagogue is now in the hands of the united Greeks. The latter had broken a small niche or chapel in the wall at the far end of the place, in which were an altar, a crucifix, candles, flowers, and offi- ciating priest. I presume the priest was conducting a special service for the benefit of the Russian pilgrims. As we passed in, he paused in the service, and, turning his back upon the altar, eyed us curiously for some moments. (To be continued next week.)

A " GALLANT " OF ELIZABETH'S ths reign of good Queen Bess the chief marks of a " gallant," as men of fashima used to be called, were his ruff and his rapier, and the deeper the ruff and the longer the rapier the more " perfect " the gall ant gay. But in couroa of time apprentices took to robbing their masters in ‘.s-,1 er to dress themselves up as 'fashionable men, an abusP which the queen tried to put down with her usual vigM:-. She in- structed a certain number of sedate citizens to ',e stationed at the various city gates, with express orders to cut off all ruffs that were above a nail in depth, and break the points of all rapiers that were more than three feet long. This stern edict doubtless led to stormy scenes on the part of those who objected to have their collars cut short, or their swords clipped, but it had its effect. —From "Little Folks Magazine" for October. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 29, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 29, 1881.

addition to the amount of the apportionments. The committee, after considering the offer, were of opinion that it would be advisable to accept it, and instructed the Town Clerk to bring the matter before the General Purposes Committee with a copy of the resolution. It was recommended that the tenders of Messrs. J. Nunner- ley and Co., for the supply of 600 tons of breakers; of Messrs. Hough and Son, for excavating and putting in bur foundations in Peter-street and Orchard-street, be accepted; and that an order for 20,000 tiles be given to Messrs. Pendlebury and Co., and also an order for two truck loads to Mr. E. Barnett. Alderman KEAN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the Workingmen's Club could not pay its apportionment. Councillor CROSFIELD : Do you mean the Workingmen's Club in Market-street? (Laughter.) Councillor PLATT: That will come in time, Mr. Crosfield. (Loud laughter.) Alderman KEAN observed that John-street would, at some future period, occupy a central position, and the building would do for offices. The minutes were passed. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The Town Hall, Part, and Baths Committee recommended that their resolution passed on the 4th August, having I reference to the office used by the inspector of the School Attendance Committee, be rescinded; and also that a new thermometer be purchased for use in the baths. The thanks of the committee were given to Dr. Kendrick for his great attention and care of the bees in Bank Park. The income for the baths for the four weeks ending October 13th was a 4s. 6d., and for the corresponding period last year £9 9s. ld. • Councillor SUTTON said he had observed that there were no drinking cups to the water fountain in the Park, and in consequence children climbed up to the top, destroying the carved stone work with their feet. It was quite time there should be cups. The MAYOR said that cups were supplied, but they had been stolen. He had no doubt others would be supplied, and probably would be again stolen. Alderman BURGESS: Is there any chance of the fountain being stolen? (Laughter.) Alderman THEWLIS : Did you say sold or stolen? Alderman BURGESS: Sold or stolen, or something else. On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman WEBSTER, the minutes were confirmed. THE REMOVAL OF FEVER PATIENTS.—THE COMMITTEE IN A FIE. It was recommended by the Sanitary Committee that in every case in which it is certified under the provisions of the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, by the Medical Officer of Health or any other legally 1 quallified medical practitioner, that any person within the borough is suffering from any of the diseasts specified in I the Act, and is:without proper lodging or accommodation en- abling the case to be properly isolated, so as to prevent the spread of the disease or to be properly treated, the Town Clerk shall on receipt of such certificate give notice requir- ing the removal of such person to the Hospital for Infectiousl Diseases, and in case the person to whom such notice is given refuses to consent to such removal or to be removed or is by reason of age, disease or otherwise incapable of giving such consent, the Town Clerk shall make application to a justice for an order for the removal of the person so suffering to such hospital as aforsaid.—lt was also recommended that the wages of William Bloomfield be increased from 263. to 30s. per week; that the teneler of Mr. Wm. Taylor, of Hay- 'dock-street, to construct a pantry and a porch to the back door of the administrative ward; that the tender of Mr. W. S. Pierpoint, to provide and fix five electricbell in the wards of the hospital, be accepted; and that the road from Winwick-road to the entrance of the works at Longford, be paved with sets. Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes. He said he hoped no gentleman would treat that long reso- lution in a trivial or light spirit. It was a serious resolution drawn up by a gentleman perfectly competent to do so, and did not involve any change, but was simply drawn on the lines of the Act of Parliament. It was thought desirable that this recommendation should be adopted in consequence of what took place at the last meeting of the Council, and the Town Clerk now felt it necessary for what had been the practice without being written, and without coming to the Council to ask for its concurrence, he should have its con- currence and approval in the future. The thing had worked exceedingly well up to the present time—(hear, hear)—and the feeling generally in the town where infectious disease showed itself was that the hospital was the place where the patients should be removed and dealt with, and the diffi- culties in removing them had, for a new Act, been trivial to a degree. Only four cases had gone to the hospital this year in which objection to removal had been raised. Councillor CROVIELD, in seconding the motion, observed that as he was the gentleman, or as some people he dared say would say the sinner, who moved the adoption of that re- commendation, he would like to explain that it was not passed as being antagonistic to the Council, but merely as a justification to the Town Clerk in performing his duties. (Hear, hear.) The committee were bound to conform to the Act of Parliament, and he believed everything they had I done had been in proper order. He thought there was a mistake in the minds of some members of the Council, in mentioning that the committee had a desire to compel people to go to the hospital. The committee had no such desire. The great majority of the cases were of poor people, who, unfortunately, had children attacked with fever, and were only too thankful to have them removed to the hospital. (Hear, hear.) The medical officer had to report in one week 21 cases as fit for the hospital. In every one of these cases the poor people were thankful to have their children taken away. The hospital and the tents that week were filled with patients, and the medical officer told them of the case of a poor woman, close on confinement, with three children ill with fever who implored him to take them into the hospital; but he could not, as the hospital and tents were full. He bad, therefore, to leave the children where they were, and he asked the Council whether they did not think that it was a mercy to the poor people of the town to have a hospital to which people could be taken? Councillor So'r'row: Certainly. (Hear, hear.) Alderman WEBSTER said he had no doubt that in cases such as that alluded to by Councillor Crosfield the patients ought to be ramoved to the hospital. It was for such cases that the hospital was established; and it was because the cases had not been entirely confined to that class that they had objected to some of the proceedings taken under the Act. On the occasion when he opposed the clause that was being canvassed in the Council before the Bill was passed, that was the point he objected to; and they were then assured that it would only be in cases where the parties were really too poor to have the accommodation for isolation provided that the powers under the Act would be enforced. Accepting that assurance, no steps were taken against it, and the clause was allowed to go into the Bill. The clause looked suspicious at the time. The Act of Parliament said the Corporation should do certain things; but the Corpora- tion had delegated that power to the committee. That being the case, he did not see what object would be gained in passing tki resolution. He suggested that it be left out. Councillor MONKS moved that the minutes of the Sani- tary Committee be confirmed, with the exception of the recommendation having reference to the removal of persons suffering from infectious disease to the hospital. So much had been said about the question that he was sorry it had been presented to them. After the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Council he was surprised that the Sani- tary Committee had passed such a motion. The fact was that the committee declined to consider the cases as they turned up, and referred them to the medical officer to make out what certificates he thought proper; and in the event of refusal to remove, the town clerk was to get a magistrate's order. Further than that, the minute would give to the town clerk and the medical officer power to do so without giving notice to the person against whom the order was sought to be made. The TOWN CLERK: No, no. Councillor MONKS: If you deny it I accept your denial. Alderman Burgess said deliberately it was so. Alderman BURGESS: I am obliged here to say I have not

passed. Councillor WOOLVALL thanked the Council for their ex- pression of opinion concerning himself. . BRIDGES OVER STREETS. At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee, on the 29th September, the following plans were approved :—Cottage, Winmarleigh-street, for Messrs Mackie, Brewtnall, and Co. • new pot shed im Milner-street, for the Whitecross Wire and Iron Company; six houses in Bat- tersby-lane, for Mr. E. J. Jameson, subject to the payment of Is. per annum for cellar area; twelve houses in Orford- lane, for Mr. G. Boardman; warehouse at Atherton Quay, for Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.; wood shed (stable) in Dixon-street, for Mr. J. E. Wright; alterations to shop in Lythgoe's-lane, for Mr. Josiah Furness ; addition to house in Latchford, Mr. E. Auckland. It was recommended that permission be given to the Whitecross Wire and Iron Co. to construct a bridge across Milner-street to connect their works, on condition that the same be constructed at a height 1 of 15 feet clear headway in the roadway, and the company pay £5 per annum for such permission, and undertaka to remove the bridge when called upon by the Corporation by six months' notice. The plan and elevation of the bridge to be submitted for the approval of the committee. Councillor BROADBENT proposed, and Councillor PLATT seconded the adoption of the minutes. I The MAYOR, referring to the recommedation respecting the bridge across Milner-street, said he would like the prin- ciple to be laid down by the Corporation that no private firms should obstruct the thoroughfares in any way. In the present instance it appeared to him that the bridge was too low. He did not think a large load of straw could get under the bridge. It was quite a new departure, and he thought it required much consideration on the part of the Corporation whether these, things should be allowed. He was not disposed to object to the recommendation if it was properly carried out. Alderman DAVIES said the Council would observe they were protecting the public interest, as there was an under- taking by the Whitecross Wire Company to remove the bridge when cilled upon at six months' notice. Councillor SUTTON said if he belonged to the firm he should consider whether it was not to his interest to have a bridge higher than 15 feet, because at any time the Corpora- tion could do away with the proposed bridge by giving notice. The company could not erect a bridge without considerable cost, and if they wanted to construct a per- manent one it would be better for them to have it much higher. Alderman BURGESS could not help thinking it was a mistake to construct a bridge even with the consent of the Council. Bridges across public streets and thoroughfares would be found to be a thing that a future Council would not tolerate for a moment; and he thought it was a mistake to introduce the principle now. It would be very much be ter if the committee took back the recommendation, and let the Council have a little more time to consider it. Councillor CROSFIELD said he thought it was very desir- able the Whitecross Company should have permission given to them to construct the bridge. Mr. Carson told him if the Company were allowed to lay a line of rails across the road and erect a bridge the probability was they would employ between 200 and 300 snore men, and he thought it was the wish of the Council to encourage manufacturers as far as possible so long as they did not interfere with the public good. He never saw a load of straw go along Milner-street' in his life, and he did not think a bridge 15 feet high would put anyone to inconvenience. Alderman CHANDLEY thought 15 feet a very low lkel for a bridge, and suggested that the Company should increase the height by 2 feet at the least. . Councillor PAIRCLOUGII supported the minutes. He was on the committee when the recommendation was passed, and he assured the Council the matter was thoroughly con- sidered. The Whitecross Company wished to have the bridge lower than 15 feet, but this the committee would not Iconsent to. Councillor WALLINGTON considered the Council would confer an advantage upon th e public by passing the recom- mendation. Alderman TnErrus was in favour of the recommendation being referred back.' Alderman KEAN and Councillor PLATT supported the minutes. Councillor Motms suggested that the minutes should be referred back, and said as to giving employment to 300 men the bridge would not make the slightest difference. If it paid the company to establish works they would do so not- withstanding die erection of a bridge. He did not see where the difficulty arose in making the bridge 16 feet high. t h aCtotuhnecwi l l obri Whitecross cEraoNs Ss C saido m ptßhney Cp oa iudn cgirl 0 us nh do ur ledn t bfeoarr tihnemlainndd out of which the street was made. Councillor BROADBENT said the matter was very carefully considered by the committee, and the borough surveyor was called in to give his opinion and advice, and after very full discussion it was unanimously decided to grant permission to erect the bridge on the terms and in accordance with the minute before them. Although he was interested in the works, he believed they all took a pride in the advancement and success of the various manufactories in Warrington, and that they were anxious as far as possible to encourage them in every way, provided they did not sacrifice the, public convenience by so doing. In this case they did not make any sadrifice of public convenience. The bridge would enable a portion of the works to be utilised, which, without the bridge, could not be utilised; and therefore it would give employment to more people. The minutes were carried.

said so. Councillor MONIES: It is either the town clerk or your- self. Considering that there were only three of us present at the committee, it ill becomes them to pass any such resoluiton in face of the one passed the night before. With reference to its being in accordance with the law, I diffe entirely. In view of the way in which the Act has recently been circled out, I object to the powers being delegated to the medical officer and town clerk. The Act has been carried out in an arbitrary manner, and it is for that reason that I oppose the resolution. I ask the Council not to stultify themselves and be over-ridden by any committee. Counciller BURGESS seconded the amendment, and said the committee might have paid some respect to the opinion expressed a month ago by every gentleman who voted for the resolution then pased. Everyone seemed to think that if, in the opinion of two medical men, the case was con- sidered to be isolated, it was not desirable to compel removal. The committee bad utterly disregarded the expression of opinion, and had flung, in the face of the Council, the resolution—that whenever the medical officer said a case must be isolated people must be brought before the mai*istrates if they would not submit to removal. The subject bad been very fully discussed in the Council Chamber, lie thought the ordinary medical attendant, from his special knowledge of the patient, was very much better able than a stranger, and ceitainly better than the Medical Officer of Health, who held such strange notions as to what conslituted isolation, to judge whether there should be a removal to the hospital. (Hear, hear,) With reference to the caso mentioned by Councillor Cros- field, the committee bad sent so many cases to the hospital that ought not to have been that they were unable to find room for one which it was really requisite should be sent for the safety of the town. He believed the manner in which the committee bad carried out the Act had resulted in the present epidemic, as a great many of the cases were con- cealed by the parents. There was a great dread of removing children to the hospital, and parents did not care to call in a doctor till it was too late to checkthe spread of infection. she had graced the proceedings of all public assemblies at which she had appeared. (Applause.) Alderman THEW'S had much pleasure in seconding the motion. All the members of the Council, as well as the . .

ratepayers of Warrington, most feel proud at the pleasing manner, the honourable position, and the straightforward line of action the Mayor had always maintained as Chief Magistrate of the Borough. (Hear, hear.) His thorough impartiality at all times, and the manner in which he had conducted the deliberations of the Council, would redound with honour to him as long as he lived. With regard to the Mayoress, they all felt how handsomely she had be- haved, and she had set an example to the future Mayoresses of Warrington, whilst adding lustre to His Worship's posi-

tion. (Ap-plause.) Alderman DAVIES observed that they could :not express all they felt towards the Mayor on that occasion, but all would acknowledge that he had filled his office in an admir- able manner, and that he had been ably supported by his dear wife. They thanked him very much, and he did not know any man who had so gracefully filled the mayoral chair. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Alderman WEBSTER said he should not like to give a silent vote on such an occasion. The dignity of the mayoral office had been upheld in a manner which had never been surpassed. The Mayoress had gracefully presided over many gatherings, and her manner of conducting the enter- tainments had been a happy idea, and tended greatly to that general feeling of delight and satisfaction in the town during the mayoralty of Alderman Pickmere. (Hear, hear.) He alluded to the one given to public elementary teachers, and hoped that on some future occasion they might meet under similar circumstances. (Applause.) Councillor CROSFIELD said he had sat in the Council under a great many mayors, but he had never sat under one who performed the duties in a better manner or with more strict impartiality than Alderman Pickmere. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CHANDLEY observed that for many years he had abstained from saying a word on these interesting occasions, as he had such a strong personal interest with the Mayor; but, lest these feelings should be misconstrued, he would add his _testimony to the very high, honourable, and 'admirable manner in which His Worship had discharged his duties during this and previous years. He had sustained the office with great dignity and hospitality, and won the Igolden, affectionate opinions of the ratepayers generally. (Hear, hear.) It might be a gratification to the Mayor to know that the public generally passed the highest enco- miums upon him. (Applause.) The proposition was carried with acclamation, after a few eulogistic observations from Alderman Kean and the Deputy Mayor. The MAYOR said it was exceedingly gratifying to his 'feelings to hear the remarks which had been made with reference to his services, as well as those of his dear wife. He felt that he did not deserve one-half that had been said; but at the same time he had endeavoured to do his best. (Hear, hear). He thanked them most heartily for the kind words they had given utterance to. He had received the greatest kindness and courtesy from all parties in the Council, and in any little difficulties which had arisen he lual been well supported. He had also to thank the Town Clerk and the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Whittle), Mr. Choc- ley, Mr. Longdin, the Chief Constable, and other officers of the town for their uniform support in the discharge of his official duties. (Applause). Alderman HoLluEs (addressing the Mayor) said to show the substantiality of the sentiments which had been expressed with reference to the manner in which he bad dis- charged his duties as chief magistrate, he (Alderman Holmes) had been asked to present to his Worship a requisition adopted at a private meeting of the Council held on Monday evening, which asked him to accept office for another year. The requisition was as follows :—" Town Hall, Warrington, 24th October, 1881.—J. R. Pickmere, Esq., Mayor of War- rington.—Dear Mr. Mayor,—Although you have expressed your desire not to accept the office of Mayor of Warrington for another year, we, in the interests of the Corporation and borough generally, venture to ask you to re-consider the matter. We feel we ask you to make great personal sacri- fices in again undertaking the office you have filled so ably and so well; but we sincerely trust that you will consent, and thus you will add to the obligations due to you from your natiye town of Warrington." The MAYOR said he could assure them that he had looked forward to that evening with a great deal of pleasure, as he thought his official duties were coming to an end. He might state what probably they were not all aware of, that he had written to Alderman Chandley, who had informed him that it was likely he would be asked to accept the office of mayor another year. He wrote Alderman Chandley a letter explaining why he could not do so, and requested him to show it to all the members of the Council. On Friday night he accidentally heard that there was to be a I meeting of the members of the Council on Monday evening, and as he was not invited he, to use a Lancashire expres- sion, "smelt a rat." (Laughter.) Alderman Holmes was kind enough on Monday night to write him to say that a meeting had been held, and that a numerously signed requisition which had been drawn up would be presented to him. He did not care to go against the feelings of the Council, and when they were all on one side the thing was half done. He would put them in the light of a jury, and as a judge he thought he must commit himself for another twelve months. (Applause.) He hoped by so doing he would not offend any member of the Council or ratepayer. I He did not think it was wise on all occasions to re-elect the same individual, because there were gentlemen in the Coun- cil and out of it who had a very proper ambition to become,' the chief magistrate of the borough, but,at the same time if the Council thought he should accept the office another Year he was perfectly willing to place himself in their hands, *and do the best he could as he had done hitherto. He was much obliged to them for this the fourth mark of their favour, and hoped that at the end of the year he would be found worthy of their choice. (Loud applause.) The Council then rose.

THE SMOKE QUESTION AT ST. HELENS. Sir ,—As several articles and letters with reference to smoke and noxious vapours in St. Helens have lately ap- peared in your contemporaries, I should be glad if you would allow me to point out that the writers seem ignorant of the fact, that chemical works are not alone responsible for the discomfort caused by these gases. In this case it does not follow that because one trade is controlled by Act of Parliament, it is the most harmful; nor does it follow that because certain processes give off a disagreeable smell they are injurious to life. The truth is that out of the three principal trades in St. Helens, two send acid gases up their chimnies which the other is obliged to condense. If these gases were estimated, it would be found that they are the chief cause ef the destruction to vegetable life in this neigh- bourhood. Let anyone calculate tke number of tons of alkali used per week by one of these trades, and the quan- tity of ore containing a large percentage of sulphur and arsenic smelted by the other. Or let anyone watch the chimnies on a clear day, and they will see light coloured smoke coming from some at intervals, while others pour out a peculiar opal smoke continuously. Up to the present time legislation on this matter has dealt with the chemical trade alone, not because it was the most injurious, but because condensation could be used without loss to the manufacturer. The present outcry seems to show that putting one trade under control is not sufficient, but it is useless to expect a better state of things until the others are dealt with in the same way. People are becoming more fastidious than they used to be. From all the large towns we hear the same out- cry against smoke, whether chemicals are used or not, and St. Helens is certainly not worse than many others. In the last few years it has visibly improved, and the streets are much brighter and cleaner, but of course when the atmosphere is dull with moisture the towta is not a pleasant place. Still other places are not much better under the same conditions. Let those who grumble try London or Manchester in a fog ; St. Helens is net worse. Something has been said about the town becoming "salubrious, hand- some, or elegant," and something was said about "what common sense demands." It might be made more salubrious, and it might be handsomer, bat elegant—who ever heard this much-abused word more misapplied ? Common sense teaches us that working towns, like working men, leave elegance to the more favoured in the land. The death rate has been spoken of, and a single week taken as an example ; but if the Medical Officer's able report for 1880 is referred to, it will be seen that eight towns, where acid vapours do not predominate, have -a higher mortality. These vapours no doubt aggravate chest affections, but against this they undoubtedly destroy the germs of other diseases. St. Helens is not well or even "fairly drained," and this being the case, the death rate would probably be higher were it not for the chemical liquors which disinfect the sewers. There is a wide difference between organic and inorganic matter, and the simile of a "slaughter-house," which was used by one of your contemporaries in connection with this subject, shows a want of knowledge which is fatal when attempting to deal with this most difficult question.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, X.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

A special meeting of the Town Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. His Worship the Mayor , (Alderman Pickmere) presided; and there were also present Alderman Thewlis, Burgess, Kean, Holmes, Webster, Davies, , and Chandlev ; Councillors Monks, Platt, Greening, Wal- lington, Caldwell, Woolfall, Brown, Fairclough, Sutton, Jeans Barker, Barker, Burgess, Litton, Broadbent, Crosfield, Fran- comb, and Dixon; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (treasurer), T. Longdiu (surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager). PROPOSED INCREASE OF POLICE : THE WATER SUPPLY AT FIRES. The minutes of the Watch Committee stated that the Town Clerk submitted the approval of the Secretary of State of the increase in the pay of Inspector Proffitt, from 30s. to £2 a week. It was recommended that the Town Clerk apply to the Secretary of State for his approval of the appointment of six additional members of the police force; and resolved that the tender of Mr. George Blackhurst, for clock for Sessions House, be accepted. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor PLATT seconded the adoption of the minutes. Alderman THEWLIS said he was very much struck when he was in London, daring the large fire in Cheapside, to see an admirable arrangement the Fire Brigade had. Each horse's collar was surrounded by bells which kept tingling as they went along, and the traffic kept clear of the fire engines as they passed over the street. He ventured to sug- gest to the committee that it would be advisable to take the arrangement into consideration. Councillor PAIRCLOUGH thought if the arrangement was adopted in a town like Warrington it would be money thrown away. The MAYOR agreed with the ex-Mayor, and pointed out that they did not keep horses specially for the fire engine. Councillor MONKS: Don't you think the shouts of the firemen on the engine have the same effect? The MAYOR: I never heard of any difficulty in getting people out of the way. Councillor SUTTON thought the Fire Brigade should have a little more practice in the management of the engines. He noticed at the fire that occurred at the Rope Works in Bewsey-road that there were about 40 minutes between the ringing of the fire ball and the getting of the engine into working order. That seemed to him to be too long as during that time the fire had burnt down one shed. If any- thing could be done to get a more efficient service he thought it was most desirable it should be done. , The MAYOR said he thought the delay referred to was owing to want of water. It appeared that in the large main there was no water. There used to be a supply of water in it for the manufacturers, who now get their water from the the river; and the water had to come from the domestic sup- ply. The town was in a dilemma in this respect, and the Corporation would have to take into consideration someday or other, this most important question. Alderman CHANDLEY hoped when the minutes containing a report of the fire were confirmed, notice would be taken of the water supply, and he thought some of the members would ban something to say about it. It was a very serious thing that the mains should not be supplied with water in all parts of the town; and he thought they would be neg- lecting their duty if they did not investigate the cause with a view to its remedy. Councillor PLATT thought this state of affairs arose from the fact that the Water Works Company endeavoured to set themselves in antagonism to the Corporation. They tried to do everything in their power to put the Corporation to in- convenience and expense. The Mayon: And I may say also the inhabitants of the town generally. The minutes were agreed to. FINANCE COMMITTEE. The minutes comprised orders for payment of accounts amounting to £3,174 ss. 41.; and in connection with Gas Department, amounting to £982 12s. Bd. Minute of the 17th October, that this bein r the time and place, of which due notice has been given, for making an Improvement Rate, and also a General Sewers Rate, in accordance with estimates already approved by the Council; the Corporation, acting by this committee, hereby makes the same accordingly, and directs that the common seal of the borough be affixed to the rates now produced. It was resolved that the tender of Messrs. Mackie, Brewtnall and Co., be accepted; and that the best thanks of this committee be tendered to Mr. Councillor Woolfall, for the valuable services rendered by him in auditing the accounts of the rate collector during the past year. AldermandlonrEs moved the confirmation of the minutes, and remarked that Councillor Woolfall still continued to audit the accounts in a manner most advantageous to the town generally. Methodist class meeting was Scriptural in its character, and bad been an invaluable means of grace to the Church in all --...... ages. Doubtless, one of the strongest arguments that could be used in support of the advantages and continuance of it was its past usefulness; and who would deny that with re- ference to their class meetings? It was also a valuable school of training for future usefuluess in the Church. Next to a succession of devoted and efficient ministers, nothing was of such importance as a supply of suitable lay agents for the subordinate offices of the Church, from whom, in turn, the ministry itself should be recruited. But, unless they had opportunities of distinguishing the most gifted, how were they to select ? The Church that lacked these opportunities ran the great risk of thrusting into her sacred offices men giftl essanduntried. In the class meeting the talent ' of future usefulness was discovered. In reply to his argu- ment, it was possible that someone might say that other 1 churches got on without the class meeting. He answered, l was it not an admitted fact that the Methodist branch of Christ's Church had realised a much higher religions life, aad had been more successful in aggressive work than any other section of the universal Church? So much so that Dr. Chalmers described it as Christianity in earnest, and much of this earnest Christian life and effort was due to their class meetings. Other sections of the Church had found this out, and the principle of the class meeting as it obtained among Methodists was being introduced into their churches. The late John A. James, one of the brightest ornaments of the Congregational body, speaking on the sub- ject said, "The class meetings are your strength and the want of them is our weakness." If they abolished their class meetings they could conceive that the financial require- ments of their connection might be met in other ways, but' they had the conviction that if such a thing did happen— and they had no fear that it would—(hear,hear)—the united wisdom of the Conference could not suggest an adequate -substitute. Mr. Kniveton then spoke of the best mode of conducting the class meeting. It was not advisable to lay •down specific rules, but their object was best gained by mentioning some of the evils that they might easily fall into, if not guarded against. It was of the utmost impor- tance for leaders to bear in mind that the object of class meetings was for the promotion of a healthy, vigorous, religious life. Numbers was not the test of success. A leader might have the largest class numerically and :vet, judged by the standpoint of religious experience, the very poorest. If the idea of the religious progress of the members escaped their attention, formality would be engendered, and i this was fatal to the success of the class meeting. Every- ' thing tending to formality should be shunned. The class meeting should be the hearth-stone of the Church. (Hear, bear.) He deprecated the stereotyped form of conducting a class where the leader always said the same thing exactly in the same was. Let them have a little variety. Why, for example, should the leader be the first to relate his ex- 1 perience ? Occasional changes would banish that monotony which the constant use of the very best form was ever liable to create. He advised the leaders to avoid as far as possible cant and conventional phrases, not to have long meetings, and to close within the hour; many class meetings word spoiled through being longer. A few weeks age he heard of a leader who met five members at seven o'clock in the even- ing, and prayed and talked until 20 minutes past eight, and then, taking out his watch, said, "Brethren, there is time for two or three to engage in prayer; pray short, ,please." (Laughter.) Capital advice to the members but it was a great pity he did not take it himself. Members could not he expected to listen with profit to five, seven, or nine religions addresses at a meeting. It grew wearisome, and, 39 John Wesley said, devotion ended, and this he asked them to avoid. Many persons were kept away from the class meetings because of the custom requiring all present to speak. It should be the aim of the leader to make every- one feel at home. They should be punctual in their atterd- ance. Each member should look upon his class as depend- ent upon himself. Others might be led by their example, and if the influence was wrong it might prove a snare of the devil to them. Outsiders often said that their leaders were inefficient, and for that reason would not join their classes. They admitted this to be so in some cases, but thank God they had leaders "who lured to brighter worlds and led the way." There was a lack of 'efficient men in every depart- ment. of the Church. Their superintendents mourned over it, and would readily avail themselves of efficient workers. These be would ask to join them. (Hear, hear.) They would grow better by the Union. The late never-be-forgotten Dr. Prinshon said, "God forbid that the day should ever dawn when the class meeting shall cease as an organised system of testimony and the badge of membership in the Methodfit branch of the Church of Christ." We may mention that six prizes and eighteen cettiticates have also been gained by the students of the Science and Art Classes in connection with the school, and will be distri- buted on a future occasion. A vote of thanks was proposed to Mr. Aspinall, by Mr. W FISHER, seconded by Mr. W. HANICINSON, and carried unani- mously. In responding, Mr. ASPINALL made some observations con- demnatory of the course pursued by some public men in using Johnsonian words in addressing public audiences. Such gentlemen reminded him of a story to the effect that a working man was ill, and his wife went to the doctor for a supply of physic. This she obtained, and was also told that it must be taken in a recumbent posture. Of course it was quite right for the doctor to use such long words as he was a very clever man. Away the poor woman ran to her neigh- bours, and asked if she could borrow a recumbent posture. At last she got to a house where they were very obliging, and the mistress told her she had such an article, but un- fortunately, she had just lent it! (Langhter.) The wife went home quite fatigued. A friend looked in shortly after- wards, and told her that she had got the very thing in the house, as her husband was the "recumbent posture," he having been lying on his bed all day. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Aspinall concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and Mr. Annett, which was passed. In acknowledging the vote, Mr. PRESTON said that Mr. Annett was the father of the proposal to have a children's concert, and he had carried out all the arrangements. Mr. ANNETT, in the course of his reply, urged upon the parents the importance of carrying out the advice given them that evening by Mr. Aspinall as to regularity and punctuality, as, from a teacher's point of view, it was very important. By so doing the parents would be doing justice to themselves' justice to the schools, justice to the mana- gers, and last but not least, justice to the teachers.
